Chapter V.5 — Critical Moments, Stronger Opponents and Predictable Mistakes

Learning objectives

  • Recognise a critical moment at the board, and know how Analysis defines one afterwards.
  • Use defensive resources, especially checks and repetition, against stronger opponents.
  • Identify your predictable mistakes from the coach's topics and the Lab, and train them away.

Prerequisites

Chapter V.1 (calculation), Book II's defence chapter, Book IV's endgame chapters.

Explanation

The game's definition. [Demonstrated] src/analysis/analyzer.ts (crown-critical-1): a position is critical when the best move is at least 0.10 expected-score points better than the second-best (or when a mate is available and the second move is not a mate). The game summary reports how many critical moments you handled (expected-score loss ≤ 0.05). At the board you have no engine, so learn the signs ([Counsel]):

  • Your opponent has just changed the position's character with a capture, a pawn break or a sacrifice.
  • You have only one or two moves that do not lose material (an "only move").
  • A pawn is two steps from promotion, which on this board happens early.
  • Checks are available for either side.

When you notice a sign, stop and spend time. The Lab's Time management dimension measures whether you do.

Against stronger opponents the honest goal is often the draw. Crown has two automatic draws you can aim for: bare kings and fivefold repetition. Threefold repetition and the 100-halfmove rule can be claimed. Perpetual check is the classic defensive weapon: if you can check forever, the position repeats ([Demonstrated], src/rules/adjudication.ts).

Predictable mistakes. [Demonstrated] src/academy/coach.ts lists the coach's topics: hanging pieces, knight forks, double attacks, mating nets, the opponent's threats before your move, promotion races, converting winning positions, and calculation. Each note is derived from an actual engine line replayed under the rules. The Lab marks a pattern as recurring only after at least 5 occurrences in at least 3 games.

Illustrated example

Academy puzzle pz-1w5drbc (goal: "Find the only move that holds", Defensive Survival pool).

[Demonstrated] 1.Rxe1+! Kxe1 and only the two kings remain: an automatic draw by bare kings (the checker confirms the final position). Black could decline the rook with a king move, but then K+R against K is lost for Black. Every other White move loses to the queen. This is a critical moment in its purest form: one move is far better than every other, and the weaker side saves the game by trading everything off.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Notice the sign: you are a queen against a rook down in material. That is a critical moment.
  2. List forcing moves first. Here a capture with check exists, and the board's draw rules (Rulebook: bare kings) make the trade a full save.
  3. Ask "what does my opponent threaten if I do nothing?" This is the coach's threat-awareness topic. It would have shown you that a quiet move loses.

Common mistakes

  • Playing fast in critical moments and slowly in quiet ones. This is the most common time-management fault in competitive play ([Counsel]).
  • Going for a perpetual too early. If the position is objectively fine, repeating throws away chances. Use the evaluation graph in later study to judge whether the draw was needed.
  • Forgetting that threefold repetition must be claimed. It is not automatic until the fifth occurrence.

Advanced insight

Against a much stronger opponent, reduce the number of critical moments you face. Every critical moment is a chance to lose. Simplifying lines (Chapter V.2) and forcing repetitions reduce them ([Counsel]). The reverse holds too: against a weaker opponent, create critical moments, because each one is a chance for them to err.

Worked example

Academy puzzle pz-1qogh9k ("Find the only move that holds", difficulty 3).

1.Nf5+ Kc4 2.Nd6+ Kd4 3.Nf5+. The knight checks from f5 and d6 in turn, and after move 3 the position after 1.Nf5+ has occurred a second time. [Demonstrated] this is the verified line of the puzzle. Continuing to repeat leads to a threefold-repetition claim (or the automatic fivefold draw). The weaker side saved half a point by spotting a defensive resource at the critical moment.

Guided exercise

Academy puzzle pz-r2s0tz (difficulty 3). White is under pressure. Look for a knight move that uncovers a check from the queen on a3, and for a square the knight can return to.

Independent exercises

  1. Academy puzzle pz-j2j4tm. Black to move. A rook against rook and pawn: find the only move that holds.
  1. Academy puzzle pz-bus7cm. White to move. Find the only move that holds, which begins with a check.
  1. Look at your last three analysed losses. For each one, write down the first ply the summary marks as a turning point. What was the sign at the board?
  2. In which situation is a threefold repetition not a draw until you claim it, and what happens on the fifth occurrence?

Answers

  • Guided: 1.Nd3+! Ke6 2.Nc5+ Kd6 3.Nd3+. This is the verified line. 1.Nd3+ is a discovered check: the knight leaves c5 and opens the a3–d6 diagonal for the queen. 2.Nc5+ is a direct knight check, and 3.Nd3+ discovers the queen again, so the position repeats. The verifier found no other move that holds.
  • V.5.1: 1…Ra6+! 2.Kd5 Ra5+. The verified line. Black checks from a distance along the ranks, so White's king cannot shelter the pawn.
  • V.5.2: 1.Qf4+! Kd5 2.Qf5+. The verified line. Queen checks with tempo against the king in the centre.
  • Exercise 3: a turning point is a ply where the evaluation crosses between "better" (expected score

    0.65), "balanced" and "worse" (< 0.35) (src/analysis/analyzer.ts). The sign at the board is your own answer.

  • Exercise 4: threefold is always only claimable. The draw becomes automatic on the fifth occurrence (fivefold repetition). The same applies to 100 halfmoves without a capture or pawn move (claimable) and 150 (automatic).

Summary

A critical moment is one where the best move is clearly better than the second, and at the board you feel it as forcing play, only moves, near-promotions and available checks. Spend your time there. Against stronger opponents, reduce critical moments and look for perpetual checks and repetitions. Learn your predictable mistakes from the coach's topics and fix them in the Academy.

Next lesson

Chapter V.6: after the game the engine becomes your mirror. How do you look into it without fooling yourself?

Chapter V.6 — The Engine's Mirror: postgame study, evaluations and losses

Learning objectives

  • Use every Analysis tool in the game: presets, candidate lines, variations, bookmarks, training retries, Replay Your Mistakes and the Lab.
  • Translate centipawns into expected score with the game's own map, and read the grades with the right caution.
  • Follow a fixed routine for analysing a loss.

Prerequisites

Chapters V.1–V.5.

Explanation

The tools. [Demonstrated] src/analysis/analyzer.ts, src/ui/AnalysisScreen.tsx, src/academy/*:

Tool What it does
Presets Quick (depth 5), Standard (depth 7, the default), Deep (depth 9; 4 candidate lines instead of 3). Deeper is slower and more reliable.
Candidate lines for each move: the best line and alternatives, each with its expected score.
Explore a variation step through a candidate line on the board; Return to Main Line goes back.
Bookmarks Bookmark Position and Mark Memorable save plies of the game for later study.
Retry from This Position (Unrated) shown on your moves that lost more than 0.05; starts an untimed training game from the position before your move, against the same opponent. Training games are never rated and are excluded from the Lab's game evidence.
Replay Your Mistakes (Academy) turns every move of yours that lost ≥ 0.12 expected score in an analysed game into a puzzle (accepting any move within 0.02 of the best).
The Lab chess skill dimensions (Tactical vision, Calculation, Positional understanding, Defensive awareness, Endgame technique, Threat recognition, Opening understanding, Time management, Decision consistency, Adaptability), each a success rate with its denominator and a 95 % interval. It says "insufficient" when there is too little evidence.

The expected-score scale. [Demonstrated] crown-outcome-map-v2 is an isotonic map fitted on 43,305 positions from engine games and validated on held-out opening families. Values for the side to move:

Engine score −500 −300 −200 −100 −50 0 +50 +100 +150 +200 +300 +500
Expected score 0.009 0.073 0.160 0.329 0.406 0.502 0.575 0.676 0.769 0.820 0.932 0.989

(Computed by calling mapV2 from src/analysis/outcomeMap.ts.) A one-pawn edge (+100) is worth about two-thirds of a point in engine games. A three-pawn edge is close to decisive. The map comes from engine games, and humans convert advantages less reliably, so read it as "how winning the position is", not "how likely you are to win".

Grades. [Demonstrated] The grading methodology is crown-grade-v3-experimental. A move's loss is the drop in expected score compared with the best move. The bins are Best ≤ 0.002, Excellent ≤ 0.02, Good ≤ 0.05, Inaccuracy ≤ 0.12, Mistake ≤ 0.25, Blunder above. The bins and the accuracy constant are uncalibrated placeholders: Accuracy = 100·exp(−4 × mean loss). Great and Brilliant labels are not validated, and Brilliant-move achievements wait for validated grading. Played Like is shown as "Calibrating" because the model failed its release gate: it did no better than a naive accuracy baseline. Treat grades as pointers to look at, not verdicts. Where a grade is uncertain between depths, the game says so.

Illustrated example

You lost a Rapid game. The summary shows two turning points (plies 23 and 31) and one Blunder at ply 31 with a loss of 0.41. The coach note on ply 31 is under Threat awareness and shows the engine line in which your opponent wins a rook.

Routine:

  1. Open ply 23 first. The first turning point is usually the real cause; the blunder is often just the consequence.
  2. Explore the best candidate at ply 23 and step through it. Can you explain in words why it is better?
  3. Bookmark ply 23, and use Retry from This Position (Unrated) to play the position again against the same opponent.
  4. After the game, open Replay Your Mistakes. Ply 31 (loss 0.41 ≥ 0.12) will be there as a puzzle.
  5. A week later, check whether the Lab's Threat recognition rate has moved, and look at its interval, not just its value.

Step-by-step reasoning: the loss routine

  1. Before the engine: write down the move where you think you went wrong, and why. (Your own view first: the comparison is the lesson.) ([Counsel])
  2. Run Standard analysis. If a critical moment is graded with an uncertainty warning, rerun with Deep.
  3. Find the first turning point, not the biggest blunder.
  4. Explain the better move in words. If you cannot, the engine line is not yet knowledge.
  5. Retry the position against the same opponent until you hold it.
  6. Classify the error by coach topic, and count it. Five occurrences in three games is a pattern.
  7. Assign training: puzzles in that theme (Tactical Academy), Defensive Survival, or the Endgame Workshop.

Common mistakes

  • Analysing only the blunder. The position was often already difficult.
  • Trusting a single grade. The bins are experimental, and the label can depend on depth.
  • Reading "+1.0" as "I should have won". +100 cp ≈ 0.68 expected score: likely, not certain.
  • Counting Brilliant labels as skill. They are not validated.
  • Using the engine during rated play. Rated play hides engine information by design, and assisted games are excluded from evidence and markets.

Advanced insight

The Lab aggregates only reports from one methodology (the most common grading id + engine build + preset) and counts the rest as excluded. If you mix Quick and Deep analyses, your Lab evidence splits. Pick one preset for your record (Standard is the default) and use Deep only for extra study ([Demonstrated], src/academy/lab.ts eligibleItems).

Worked example

A move goes from +150 (expected 0.769) to +50 (0.575) after your reply, while the best move would have kept +150. Loss = 0.769 − 0.575 = 0.194 → Mistake (0.12 < 0.194 ≤ 0.25), and it qualifies for Replay Your Mistakes (≥ 0.12). In words: you turned a large edge (about three-quarters of a point) into a small one (just over half).

Guided exercise

Your move took the position from 0 cp to −100 cp; the best move kept 0. (a) Compute the loss. (b) Which grade? (c) Does it become a Replay Your Mistakes puzzle?

Independent exercises

  1. +300 → +200 with the best move keeping +300. Loss and grade?
  2. −50 → −200 with the best keeping −50. Loss and grade?
  3. Your mean loss over a game is 0.05. What accuracy does the game report?
  4. Why should a fast drop from +500 to +300 worry you less than a drop from +50 to −100?

Answers

  • Guided: (a) 0.502 − 0.329 = 0.173. (b) Mistake. (c) Yes (≥ 0.12).
  • 1: 0.932 − 0.820 = 0.112 → Inaccuracy (0.05 < 0.112 ≤ 0.12).
  • 2: 0.406 − 0.160 = 0.246 → Mistake (just under 0.25).
  • 3: 100·exp(−4 × 0.05) = 100·exp(−0.2) ≈ 81.9.
  • 4: in expected score, +500 → +300 is 0.989 → 0.932 (−0.057), while +50 → −100 is 0.575 → 0.329 (−0.246). The scale is flat near decisive positions and steep near balance.

Summary

Use presets, candidate lines, variations, bookmarks and retries to turn a lost game into training. Read centipawns through the expected-score map. Treat grades as experimental pointers. Brilliant is unvalidated and Played Like is Calibrating. Start with the first turning point, explain the better move in words, and train the pattern until the Lab's interval moves.

Next lesson

Chapter V.7: a repertoire built on the balanced openings the engine itself trains on.

Chapter V.7 — The Sixty-Four Gates: building a repertoire

Learning objectives

  • Know the 64 balanced two-ply openings in tools/bench/openings.json and what "balanced" means there.
  • Build a small, coherent repertoire for White and Black.
  • Attach a long-term plan to each opening instead of memorising moves.

Prerequisites

Book III's opening and pawn-structure chapters.

Explanation

[Demonstrated] The engine's benchmark book has 64 two-ply openings (one White move, one Black reply), chosen because Fairy-Stockfish at depth 10 judged each within ±80 cp from White's view. They range from −76 to +76 (mean +16). The game's opening classifier (crown-open-0) names them descriptively. No established 6×6 opening theory exists, and the Lab's Opening understanding dimension measures soundness (loss ≤ 0.05 in the opening phase), not memorised lines.

White's ten first moves and the replies in the book, with the evaluation (cp, White's view):

White's first move Book replies (eval)
Nc3 a4 (−53), e4 (−74), Nc4 (0), Na4 (+15), Nf4 (−23), Nd4 (0)
Na3 a4 (+45), d4 (+7), e4 (−14), Nc4 (+7), Nf4 (+22)
Nf3 a4 (+14), b4 (+14), c4 (−30), d4 (−30), f4 (+30), Nf4 (+76), Nd4 (+22)
Nd3 a4 (+61), b4 (−46), f4 (−76), Nc4 (+71), Na4 (+38), Nd4 (+7)
a3 a4 (+38), c4 (−59), d4 (−23), e4 (+75), f4 (0), Nc4 (+75), Na4 (−17), Nf4 (+30), Nd4 (+69)
b3 a4 (−51), b4 (+75), c4 (−22), d4 (+23), e4 (+71), f4 (+7), Nf4 (+14)
c3 b4 (0), c4 (−7), d4 (+45), f4 (+67), Na4 (+72), Nf4 (+53)
d3 b4 (+15), c4 (0), d4 (+46), e4 (+22), f4 (+67), Nf4 (+76)
e3 a4 (−46), b4 (−23), e4 (+67), Na4 (+36)
f3 a4 (+60), b4 (−7), c4 (+52), d4 (−38), e4 (+75), f4 (−23), Na4 (+56), Nf4 (0)

(Converted from the book's move codes to SAN by replaying each line under the rules.) Two things matter. First, every pawn move is a single step: there is no double step on this board. Second, after one move each, the pawns are already one or two steps from contact.

Illustrated example

After 1.Nc3 e4 Black's e-pawn already attacks d3 and f3, the squares White's d- and f-pawns would step to. It is three steps from promotion. For Black this is a good choice against Nc3. For White it is a reason to choose another first move.

Step-by-step reasoning: building a repertoire

  1. White: choose one or two first moves. Pick ones where most book replies are ≥ 0, so that Black's best reply still leaves you a playable game. For example, d3 (lowest reply 0) or c3 (lowest −7).
  2. Black: prepare one reply to each of White's ten first moves. Choose the most negative eval from White's view, if you understand the resulting structure. Example: against Nc3, …e4 (−74); against Nd3, …f4 (−76); against a3, …c4 (−59); against b3, …a4 (−51); against e3, …a4 (−46); against f3, …d4 (−38).
  3. Attach a plan, not a move list: for each line write one sentence. Which pawn will advance, where my knights go, where my king is safe.
  4. Test it: play training games from each line against L5–L7 and check the Lab's Opening understanding dimension.

Common mistakes

  • Treating ±76 cp as a big difference. Read through the game's expected-score map (fitted for the Crown engine, so only a rough guide for another engine's centipawns), it is about 0.37–0.63 at the extremes, and these are depth-10 judgements. Either side can play all 64 lines.
  • Memorising moves beyond move 3. There is no theory to memorise. Your plan matters more.
  • Ignoring the styled opponents' preferences. A Tactical or Positional competitor picks among its own 30 cp book for six plies (Chapter V.3).

Advanced insight

Long-term plans on 6×6. With only four steps to promotion, a pawn majority on one wing is a much more immediate asset than in orthodox chess. Middlegame plans often come down to "which majority promotes first, and whose king is closer" ([Counsel], consistent with the coach's promotion-race topic). Choose openings whose pawn structure gives you the faster majority.

Worked example

A Black repertoire against 1.Nf3. The book's replies range from −30 (…c4, …d4) to +76 (…Nf4). Choose 1…c4 or 1…d4 (−30 each). Plan for 1…d4: the pawn gains space and attacks c3 and e3 at once. Develop the knights towards the queenside, keep the king on d6 until the centre clears, and aim the c-pawn at White's queenside. Avoid 1…Nf4 (+76), the worst book reply for Black.

Guided exercise

Build a White repertoire with one first move. Pick it from the table so that Black's best book reply is as good as possible for White. Which move, and what is Black's best book reply?

Independent exercises

  1. Which first move for White has the most book replies, and what is its worst one for White?
  2. Against 1.f3, which book reply is best for Black, and which is worst?
  3. Why might a player prefer 1.c3 (worst reply −7) over 1.Na3 (worst reply −14) even though the difference is tiny?
  4. Write a one-sentence plan for White after 1.d3 d4.

Answers

  • Guided: d3 or c3. 1.d3's lowest book reply is 0 (…c4). 1.c3's lowest is −7 (…c4). Choose d3 for the strict answer: Black's best book reply leaves 0.
  • 1: a3 with 9 replies; its worst for White is …c4 (−59).
  • 2: best for Black …d4 (−38); worst for Black …e4 (+75).
  • 3: with a gap of only 7 cp, choose by structure and plan: which middlegames you understand. Both are balanced.
  • 4: any concrete plan is acceptable. For example: "The d-pawns block each other. I will develop Nf3 and challenge the d4-pawn with e3, keeping my king on d1 behind the blocked centre until the queens come off."

Summary

The 64 book openings are all balanced at depth 10 (±80 cp). Choose a small repertoire by the worst reply you might face, attach a plan to each line, and test it in training games. There is no 6×6 theory, so understanding beats memory.

Next lesson

Chapter V.8: the final challenge, Sovereign Unbound, described exactly as it is.

Chapter V.8 — The Unbound Challenge: preparing to face Sovereign Unbound

Learning objectives

  • Know exactly what Sovereign Unbound is, what its thinking budgets mean, and how strong it has been measured to be.
  • Set honest goals for games against it.
  • Prepare with the game's tools rather than with myths.

Prerequisites

All of Book V.

Explanation

What it is. [Demonstrated] src/engine/levels.ts: L9 Sovereign Unbound is the canonical engine (crown-search-2 + crown-eval-4). It has no random choices, no handicap and no style, uses a 2^20-entry transposition table (about 11.5 MB), and plays with a thinking budget you choose:

Budget Name Notes
1 s Fast casual
5 s Strong casual
10 s Rated rated games always use 10 s, so its rating stays meaningful
15 s Deep casual
30 s Unbound casual
60 s Unbound+ casual

The budget is an upper bound per move: in timed games the engine's own clock can lower it. Its allocation is min(budget, (remaining − reserve)/22 + 0.75 × increment, 0.35 × remaining). At the first move of a Blitz 3+2 game that is about 9.6 s, in Rapid 5+3 about 15.8 s, and in Classical 15+10 about 48.3 s. So the 30 s and 60 s budgets only take full effect in untimed games or with plenty of clock. (Computed from allocateTime, with a reserve of min(10 % of remaining, 1.5 s).) Since v0.8, fullBudget makes the engine keep starting new search iterations until 62.5 % of its budget is used. At a 5 s budget it was measured using about 81 % of the time.

How strong. [Demonstrated] src/engine/calibration.json and docs/V8_SOVEREIGN_STANDARD.md:

  • Crown rating 3038 ± 171: a derived point (L8's rating plus a measured L9 − L8 difference of +112 [60, 163] over 64 games at time-scaled budgets on one host). It is engine-vs-engine only. There are no human calibration games. The Crown scale is not FIDE.
  • More time helps: in 128-game matches against itself, each doubling of thinking time was worth +103 [55, 153] (50 → 100 ms), +80 [38, 128] (100 → 200 ms) and +106 [63, 150] (200 → 400 ms) Elo. The gain at multi-second budgets was not measured (doubling gains usually shrink as time grows). So 15/30/60 s are genuinely stronger than 1/5 s, but by an unknown amount.
  • Against Fairy-Stockfish (a developer benchmark, never bundled), at equal time it scored −379 [−482, −309] Elo at 100 ms, −330 at 300 ms and −283 [−379, −213] at 1,000 ms. Sovereign is strong on the Crown scale, and far from the strongest possible 6×6 player.

What that means for you. The calibration's logistic model gives the expected score per game for a rating gap d as 1/(1 + 10^(d/400)): for d = 400, 0.091; d = 600, 0.031; and for a 2000-rated player against 3038 (d = 1038), about 0.0025, roughly one draw in two hundred games. Treat this as order-of-magnitude only: the rating has an RD of 171, and it says nothing about humans directly. Honest goal-setting: below about 2600 on the Crown scale, aim to survive critical moments and to reach drawn endings. A draw against Sovereign Unbound is a real achievement. A win is extraordinary ([Counsel] on goals; the numbers are [Demonstrated]).

Illustrated example

The step from L8 to L9 is measured, about +112 Elo. The step from L9 at 10 s to L9 at 60 s is not. When you beat L9 at the Fast budget (1 s), you have beaten a weaker opponent than rated L9. The 5 s and 10 s budgets differ by one doubling, which at short budgets was worth about +80 to +106. Record the budget with every result.

Step-by-step reasoning: the preparation cycle

  1. Climb the ladder honestly: reach a positive score against L7, then L8, before you play rated L9 ([Counsel]).
  2. Play casual L9 games at 1 s to learn its style: it never errs randomly, so every inaccuracy you see is in your play.
  3. Study each loss with the routine in Chapter V.6. Against L9, the first turning point is usually early.
  4. Choose openings from Chapter V.7 that lead to structures you understand.
  5. Aim for simplification and repetition (Chapters V.2 and V.5). Fewer critical moments means fewer chances to go wrong.
  6. Then play rated L9 at 10 s, in a time control that gives you enough clock: Classical 15+10 if you calculate slowly.

Common mistakes

  • Believing longer budgets are "unbeatable". They are stronger, by an unmeasured amount. They are not perfect.
  • Believing short budgets are "weak". At 1 s it is still a full search with no randomness.
  • Hoping it will "throw" a game. No level does. L9 has no selection at all.
  • Comparing Crown ratings with FIDE ratings. The scale is anchored at L1 = 800 by design.

Advanced insight

Engines are strongest in sharp tactics and relatively weaker in long-horizon plans. Their weakness is the search horizon, not calculation. On a 6×6 board the horizon covers more of the game than on 8×8, so expect fewer strategic gifts than in orthodox engine games ([Counsel]: a plausible reading of the depth figures, not a measurement). In rated play you get no engine hints. Your preparation is all you bring.

Worked example

You are 2,250 (established) and play 10 rated games against L9. Logistic expected score per game for d = 788: 1/(1 + 10^(788/400)) ≈ 0.011, so about 0.1 points over 10 games. Expect to lose most games. Each game is still a lesson, and each draw is a clear signal of progress. Afterwards, Glicko-2 moves your rating little for expected losses and a lot for a surprise draw.

Guided exercise

At the first move of a Rapid 5+3 game you select the 30 s budget. (a) How long can L9 think on its first move? (b) Which budget would give the same first-move limit? (c) Why might you still choose 30 s?

Independent exercises

  1. Which budget do rated L9 games always use, and why?
  2. Using the doubling table, estimate the Elo difference between 100 ms and 400 ms thinking. Why can you not apply the same figure to 15 s versus 60 s?
  3. In Classical 15+10, with 300 s left and a 10 s increment, how long can L9 think if you chose 60 s?
  4. Name two things L9 never does that some lower levels do.

Answers

  • Guided: (a) about 15.8 s (the clock allocation is below the 30 s budget). (b) Any budget ≥ 15.8 s gives the same first move. The 15 s budget gives slightly less (15 s). (c) Later in the game, if the engine has saved time or with a larger increment, the allocation could rise above 15 s. The 30 s budget sets the upper bound.
  • 1: 10 s (MAX_RATED_BUDGET_S), so that its measured rating stays meaningful.
  • 2: about +80 + 106 = +186 Elo for two doublings at those budgets. The multi-second gain was not measured, and doubling gains usually shrink as time grows.
  • 3: reserve = min(30 s, 1.5 s) = 1.5 s; (300 − 1.5)/22 + 0.75 × 10 = 13.57 + 7.5 ≈ 21.1 s (below the 0.35 × 300 = 105 s cap and below 60 s).
  • 4: it never chooses randomly among near-best moves (L1–L4 do), and it never limits its search to a fixed node budget (L5–L7 do). It also never uses a style repertoire.

Summary

Sovereign Unbound is the full canonical engine with a chosen budget (rated: 10 s). Its rating is 3038 ± 171 (derived, engine games only). More time makes it stronger, by an unmeasured amount at long budgets, and it remains well below Fairy-Stockfish. Prepare by climbing the ladder, studying losses, simplifying and repeating. Set honest goals: a draw is a triumph.

Next lesson

Book VI, The Oracle: the other half of a Sovereign's mind, forecasting under uncertainty on the Crown Exchange.

Book VI — The Oracle

Forecasting and the Crown Exchange

A Sovereign who can calculate a mate in three but cannot say how likely a game is to end in a draw has learned only half of judgement. The Oracle's discipline is the other half: stating beliefs as numbers, testing them against reality, and never staking more than the evidence supports.

Fictional money only. The Crown Exchange uses the game's fictional dollars. Nothing in it is, or can become, real money, and nothing in this book is advice about real-money betting or investing. The Exchange is in the game to teach probability, calibration and risk. Its lessons are the same ones that make reckless real-world gambling a losing proposition, and this book says so wherever it matters.

As in Book V, statements are marked [Demonstrated] (read from the game's code or computed with its own functions) or [Counsel] (practical advice, not measured). Every dollar figure in a worked example was computed by calling the game's own pricing code (src/exchange/lmsr.ts) unless stated otherwise.

The rules this book relies on. [Demonstrated] (src/exchange/*, src/app/federation.ts, src/app/markets.ts):

  • A market lists mutually exclusive, exhaustive states, for example White wins / Draw / Black wins. A share of a claim pays $1 if the claim's state happens and $0 otherwise.
  • Prices come from an automated market maker, the LMSR. There is no order book, and you trade against the maker.
  • A fee of 1 % of the executed amount (rounded up) is charged on every buy and every sell.
  • Holdings are long-only: you can sell only shares you hold. There is no short selling.
  • Markets go open → closed → settled or cancelled, and are never reopened. Settlement pays $1 per winning share. Cancellation pays the market's published cancellation vector (for a match market, $1/3 per share).
  • Information policy: official markets never list your own games. Rated games never carry markets. If you sponsor a competitor, you cannot buy in markets involving them (you may still sell). If you enter an event, its open winner market is cancelled at 1/n first. In live games, move grades stay hidden until the market is settled or cancelled. There is also a separate Sandbox Exchange with practice money on your own casual quick matches, where you may only back yourself and trading closes at the first move. Sandbox money never touches your official cash, net worth, ratings or standings.

Chapter VI.1 — The Language of Chance: probability, prices and expected value

Learning objectives

  • Read a price as an implied probability.
  • Compute the expected value (EV) of a trade in dollars, including the fee.
  • Find the break-even belief for a trade.

Prerequisites

Basic arithmetic with decimals. Book V, Chapter V.6 (the expected-score scale).

Explanation

A probability is a number from 0 to 1 that says how likely an outcome is. For a single game, the three outcomes White wins, Draw, Black wins have probabilities that add up to 1.

Because a share pays exactly $1 if its outcome happens, a price of $0.40 says "40 % likely". That is the implied probability. In the LMSR the prices of all states always add up to exactly $1 ([Demonstrated], prices() normalises them). The price of a claim covering several states is the sum of their prices.

The expected value of a trade is what it earns on average, if your belief is right:

EV = (your probability) × $1 × shares − (total paid, including the fee)

For a small trade at price p, the total paid per share is about p × 1.01, so the trade has positive EV only if your belief q is above 1.01 × p. That is the break-even belief. For larger trades the price moves against you while you buy (Chapter VI.2), and the break-even rises.

Illustrated example

A featured match is priced White $0.40 · Draw $0.30 · Black $0.30. You believe White wins 50 % of the time.

You buy 10 White shares. The game's quote is $4.14 in total, fee included (computed with buyClaimMicro and feeMicro; the price after your trade is $0.420).

EV = 0.50 × $10 − 4.14 =  *  * +0.86**. If White wins you receive $10.00 (profit $5.86). Otherwise you receive $0 (loss $4.14). Neither result tells you whether the trade was good. The EV does, and only if your 50 % is right.

Step-by-step reasoning

  1. Write your probability first, before you look at the price ([Counsel]: this guards against anchoring).
  2. Read the price as the market's implied probability.
  3. Compare: is your belief above 1.01 × price?
  4. Get the quote for the size you want. It includes the price movement and the fee.
  5. Compute EV = belief × shares − quoted total.
  6. Decide size separately (Chapter VI.4). A positive EV does not mean "buy as much as you can".

Common mistakes

  • Treating the price as the probability of winning money. The price is the probability of the outcome. Your profit also depends on what you paid.
  • Forgetting the draw. In chess-like games draws are common. The Federation's result model gives about 31 % draws between equals ([Demonstrated], crown-result-model-1, ν = 0.9).
  • Forgetting the fee on the way out. Selling also costs 1 %.

Advanced insight

The Federation's public forecast for a match uses the Davidson model on public ratings ([Demonstrated], src/federation/resultModel.ts): with π = 10^(rating/400) for each side, P(W) = π_w / Z, P(D) = ν·√(π_w·π_b) / Z, P(B) = π_b / Z, where Z is the sum of the three numerators and ν = 0.9. Computed values:

White − Black (public rating) P(White) P(Draw) P(Black) White's expected score
0 0.345 0.310 0.345 0.500
+100 0.447 0.302 0.251 0.598
+200 0.549 0.278 0.174 0.688
+400 0.722 0.206 0.072 0.825

Prices that stray from this public model are either noise or information. Chapter VI.7 shows which.

Worked example

A promotion market (Yes / No) shows Yes at $0.30. You think the competitor's chance of finishing in the top two is 40 %.

  • Break-even for a small trade: 1.01 × 0.30 = 0.303. Your 0.40 is above it.
  • Quote for 25 Yes shares (liquidity b = 80 for promotion markets): $8.44 total, average price $0.334, price after $0.369 (computed).
  • EV = 0.40 × $25 − 8.44 =  *  * +1.56**.

Guided exercise

A match is priced White $0.55 · Draw $0.25 · Black $0.20. (a) What probability does the market give a Black win? (b) What is the break-even belief for a small purchase of Black shares? (c) You believe Black wins 25 % of the time, and the quote for 20 Black shares is $4.25. What is the EV?

Independent exercises

  1. The draw is priced at $0.31. A small trade costs about $0.313 per share with the fee. What is the lowest belief in a draw at which buying is worth it?
  2. You buy 1 share of White in a fresh match market (all prices $1/3). The game's quote is $0.3376. Why is it more than $0.3333?
  3. You hold 20 White shares bought for $9.00 in total. White wins. What is your profit? What would it have been if the game had been cancelled (match markets pay $1/3 per share)?
  4. Explain in one sentence why "the trade lost money" is not the same as "the trade was a mistake".

Answers

  • Guided: (a) 20 %. (b) 0.202 (1.01 × 0.20). (c) EV = 0.25 × $20 − 4.25 =  *  * +0.75**.
  • 1: about 0.313. Below that, the fee makes the expected profit negative even before price movement.
  • 2: the price rises slightly while you buy (the cost is 0.334261fortheshareitself), andthe1(0.003343, rounded up) is added. Total $0.337604, which the screen shows rounded.
  • 3: win: $20 − 9 =  *  * +11**. Cancellation: 20 × $1/3 = 6.67(roundeddownperholding), so *  * −2.33**.
  • 4: a trade's quality is its EV at the time of the trade, given what was knowable. Its result also includes luck (Chapter VI.7).

Summary

Price = implied probability. EV = belief × payout − total cost. Break-even belief ≈ 1.01 × price for small trades, higher for large ones. Write your belief before you look at the price, and judge trades by EV, not by results.

Next lesson

Chapter VI.2: how the market maker sets those prices, and why buying moves them.

Chapter VI.2 — The Engine of Prices: the LMSR market maker, liquidity and slippage

Learning objectives

  • State the LMSR cost and price formulas and compute a trade's cost by hand.
  • Explain liquidity (b), slippage and the maker's funded subsidy.
  • Estimate price impact before you trade.

Prerequisites

Chapter VI.1. Natural logarithms and exponentials (a calculator is fine).

Explanation

[Demonstrated] src/exchange/lmsr.ts: the Crown Exchange uses Hanson's logarithmic market scoring rule with a fixed liquidity parameter b. For outstanding shares q = (q₁, …, qₙ) across the n states:

Cost function: C(q) = b · ln( Σᵢ e^(qᵢ / b) )

Price of state i: pᵢ = e^(qᵢ / b) / Σⱼ e^(qⱼ / b)

Cost of a trade that changes q to q′: C(q′) − C(q)

Consequences:

  • Buying a state raises its price and lowers the others. Prices always add up to 1.
  • Path independence: buying 30 shares at once costs the same as buying 10 three times (apart from rounding and the fee on each trade).
  • Rounding favours the market: buy costs are rounded up to the next micro-dollar and sale proceeds down.
  • The maker's worst-case loss is b · ln n, and that subsidy is funded before the market opens. For a match market (b = 120, n = 3) it is $131.83.
  • Liquidity by market family: match 120, tournament winner 150, promotion 80, qualification 80, season title 100, bracket 100; Sandbox 60 (src/exchange/families.ts, src/app/federation.ts).

A larger b means more liquidity: prices move less per share. Slippage is the difference between the price you see and the average price you pay. Near a price p, each share moves the price by about p(1 − p)/b.

Illustrated example

A fresh match market: q = (0, 0, 0), b = 120, all prices $0.3333. You buy 30 White shares.

  • C(0,0,0) = 120 · ln 3 = 131.8335
  • C(30,0,0) = 120 · ln(e^0.25 + 2) = 120 · ln(3.284025) = 142.6884
  • Cost = 142.6884 − 131.8335 = $10.8549 (the game's exact figure: $10.854918)
  • Fee: 1 % rounded up = 0.108550 * *,sothetotalis * *10.963468
  • New White price = e^0.25 / (e^0.25 + 2) = 1.284025 / 3.284025 = 0.3910 * *;DrawandBlackfallto * *0.3045
  • Average price paid: 10.8549/30 =  * *0.3618**, about 2.9 cents of slippage per share

Step-by-step reasoning: estimating impact before trading

  1. Read the current price p and the market's b.
  2. Estimate the price after n shares: about p + n·p(1 − p)/b for small n. Near $0.50 with b = 120, that is about 0.2 cents per share.
  3. The average price you pay is roughly halfway between the start and the end price.
  4. Ask the game for the exact quote. The estimate only tells you whether the size is sensible.

Measured slippage when White is at $0.40 (Draw and Black $0.30), b = 120 (computed):

Shares bought Total incl. fee Average price White price after
50 $22.78 $0.451 $0.503
100 $50.78 $0.503 $0.605
150 $83.78 $0.553 $0.699
200 $121.18 $0.600 $0.779
250 $162.20 $0.642 $0.843

Common mistakes

  • Judging a trade by the displayed price. You pay the average price over the trade. Use the quote.
  • Buying and selling back quickly. A round trip costs two fees. Buying 10 shares at $0.50 costs $5.1552, and selling them straight back nets 5.0531 :  * *0.10 lost** for nothing.
  • Forgetting quotes expire. A quote is tied to the market's revision, which changes with every trade and every published live move. A stale quote is rejected, not filled at a worse price ([Demonstrated], revisionOf).

Advanced insight

Because every claim in a market shares one inventory, prices stay coherent across claims. In a bracket market (8 states: the possible final-four paths), "A is champion" covers 2 states and "A reaches the final" covers 4, so the champion claim can never cost more than the finalist claim ([Demonstrated], src/exchange/market.ts). In a fresh bracket market every path costs 1/8, so the champion claim starts at $0.25.

Worked example

How large can a trade be before it stops making sense? White is at $0.40 and you believe 0.50. As you buy, the marginal price rises towards your belief. Buying beyond the point where the marginal price passes your belief (minus the fee) loses EV. Computed EV, belief 0.50:

Shares Total paid EV Price after
10 $4.14 +$0.86 $0.420
25 $10.74 +$1.76 $0.451
40 $17.80 +$2.20 $0.482
50 $22.78 +$2.22 $0.503
60 $27.96 +$2.04 $0.524
75 $36.13 +$1.37 $0.555
100 $50.78 −$0.78 $0.605

EV peaks at about 45–50 shares (the price needed to reach $0.495 is 46 shares). Beyond that, every extra share costs more than it is worth to you. The market's liquidity, not your enthusiasm, sets the useful size.

Guided exercise

A fresh match market (b = 120). (a) Compute the White price after buying 120 White shares. (b) Compute the cost before the fee. Use e ≈ 2.71828. (c) Is the average price above or below $0.45?

Independent exercises

  1. What subsidy does the game fund when it opens a binary promotion market (b = 80, n = 2)? And a 16-entrant tournament-winner market (b = 150)?
  2. The same 30-share purchase in a Sandbox market (b = 60) costs $11.75 before the fee and moves White to $0.452. Why is it more expensive than in a match market?
  3. Near a price of $0.50 in a b = 80 market, roughly how far does one share move the price?
  4. You sell 30 White shares straight back into the market right after the illustrated example's purchase. The proceeds are $10.854917 before the fee. Why one micro-dollar less than you paid?

Answers

  • Guided: (a) e/(e + 2) = 2.71828/4.71828 ≈ 0.5761 *  * .(b)120 · ln((e+2)/3) = 120 · ln(1.57276) ≈  * *54.34 (the game: $54.339892). (c) 54.34/120 ≈  * *0.453**, slightly above $0.45.
  • 1: 80·ln 2 = 55.45 *  * .150 · ln16 =  * *415.89 (computed with subsidyMicro, rounded up).
  • 2: a smaller b means lower liquidity: each share moves the price more, so the average price is higher.
  • 3: 0.5 × 0.5 / 80 ≈ 0.003, about 0.3 cents per share.
  • 4: buy costs round up and sale proceeds round down to the micro-dollar, so rounding residue always stays with the market's collateral. The fee is charged again on the sale, giving net proceeds of $10.746367.

Summary

The LMSR prices states by pᵢ = e^(qᵢ/b)/Σe^(qⱼ/b) and charges C(q′) − C(q) for a trade. Liquidity b sets the slippage, about p(1 − p)/b per share. The maker's loss is capped at b·ln n, funded in advance. Size your trade by where the marginal price meets your belief, not by your budget.

Next lesson

Chapter VI.3: how good are your beliefs? The game measures them.

Chapter VI.3 — Measuring the Oracle: calibration and the Brier score

Learning objectives

  • Compute the Brier score and the log score exactly as the game does.
  • Explain why honest forecasts score best (proper scoring).
  • Read the calibration chart and the skill tiers, and know how many forecasts it takes to judge them.

Prerequisites

Chapter VI.1.

Explanation

Paper forecasts. [Demonstrated] src/app/forecasting.ts (crown-forecast-1): for any market you may record a free probability vector over its states. It costs nothing and is locked when the market closes. On resolution it is scored with two proper scoring rules:

Brier score: B = Σₛ (pₛ − yₛ)², summed over all states, from 0 (perfect) to 2 (worst). Lower is better.

Log score: L = −Σₛ yₛ · ln max(pₛ, 0.001). Lower is better.

Here y is the resolution vector: 1 for the state that happened and 0 for the others (½/½ for joint champions). Cancelled markets are not scored. Because the game sums over every state, a two-state market's Brier score is twice the "binary Brier" you may know from elsewhere.

Your forecasts are compared with two baselines: the market price at the time of your forecast, and the public forecast (the model). Over your scored forecasts the game shows a tier ([Demonstrated], src/ui/ForecastScreen.tsx): Apprentice (fewer than 10 scored), Sharp (your mean Brier more than 0.02 below the public forecast's), Calibrated (within ±0.02 of it) or Learning (more than 0.02 behind it). A rolling chart shows your mean Brier over your last 10 resolved forecasts.

Calibration means that things you call 70 % happen about 70 % of the time. The game pools every (probability, outcome) pair into ten bins (0–10 %, 10–20 %, …) and shows each bin's observed frequency with a Wilson 95 % interval. A wide interval means too few forecasts in that bin to judge.

Forecast skill is never mixed into chess or financial prestige. A good forecast is not a profitable trade. Trading profit depends on prices paid and fees, and is reported separately.

Illustrated example

You forecast a match White 0.50 · Draw 0.30 · Black 0.20. Computed with the game's brier and logScore:

Result Brier Log
White wins (0.5−1)² + 0.3² + 0.2² = 0.38 −ln 0.5 = 0.693
Draw 0.5² + (0.3−1)² + 0.2² = 0.78 −ln 0.3 = 1.204
Black wins 0.5² + 0.3² + (0.2−1)² = 0.98 −ln 0.2 = 1.609

For comparison: the "know-nothing" forecast (⅓, ⅓, ⅓) always scores 0.667. A confident miss such as (0.90, 0.05, 0.05) when Black wins scores 1.715 (log 2.996). The same forecast when White wins scores 0.015.

Step-by-step reasoning: why honesty wins

Suppose a promotion is truly 70 % likely. Your expected Brier score (two-state, as the game computes it):

  • say 0.70: 0.7 × 0.18 + 0.3 × 0.98 = 0.42
  • say 0.90 (overconfident): 0.50
  • say 0.50 (timid): 0.50

Any distortion, in either direction, worsens the expected score ([Demonstrated] arithmetic). That is what "proper scoring rule" means: your best strategy is to report what you actually believe.

Common mistakes

  • Judging yourself on a handful of forecasts. For an honest forecaster facing 60 % events, the standard deviation of the mean Brier is about 0.062 over 10 forecasts, 0.028 over 50 and 0.014 over 200 (computed). The ±0.02 band between "Sharp", "Calibrated" and "Learning" needs well over 50 forecasts to mean much.
  • Rounding to 0 or 1. The log score clamps at 0.001, but a near-zero forecast that misses still scores −ln 0.001 ≈ 6.9.
  • Copying the market price. You will match the market's Brier, which is safe, but you learn nothing about your own judgement.

Advanced insight

Calibration and sharpness are different. A forecaster who always says (⅓, ⅓, ⅓) is perfectly calibrated in a trivial sense but scores 0.667 every time. Skill is being calibrated and confident when the evidence allows. The bins show calibration, and the mean Brier against the public forecast shows whether you add anything ([Counsel] on interpretation; the measures are [Demonstrated]).

Worked example

Five resolved forecasts on match markets:

Your forecast (W/D/B) Result Brier
0.50 / 0.30 / 0.20 White 0.38
0.40 / 0.35 / 0.25 Draw 0.16 + 0.4225 + 0.0625 = 0.645
0.60 / 0.25 / 0.15 White 0.16 + 0.0625 + 0.0225 = 0.245
0.30 / 0.30 / 0.40 White 0.49 + 0.09 + 0.16 = 0.74
0.45 / 0.30 / 0.25 Black 0.2025 + 0.09 + 0.5625 = 0.855

Mean = (0.38 + 0.645 + 0.245 + 0.74 + 0.855)/5 = 0.573. That beats the uniform 0.667. Whether it beats the public forecast depends on its scores on the same five markets, and five forecasts are far too few to say (see above).

Guided exercise

A two-state qualification market. You forecast Yes 0.80. (a) Brier if Yes happens? (b) Brier if No happens? (c) Your expected Brier if the true chance is 0.80?

Independent exercises

  1. Compute the Brier and log scores of (0.25, 0.50, 0.25) when the game is drawn.
  2. Why does a cancelled market not count against your forecasting record?
  3. You have 12 scored forecasts with mean Brier 0.52; the public forecast has 0.55 on the same markets. Which tier does the game show, and how much should you trust it?
  4. In your calibration chart the 70–80 % bin shows a frequency of 0.50 with a Wilson interval of 0.24–0.76. What can you conclude?

Answers

  • Guided: (a) (0.8 − 1)² + (0.2 − 0)² = 0.08. (b) 0.8² + (0.2 − 1)² = 1.28. (c) 0.8 × 0.08 + 0.2 × 1.28 = 0.32.
  • 1: Brier 0.0625 + 0.25 + 0.0625 = 0.375; log −ln 0.5 = 0.693.
  • 2: a cancelled market has no outcome. The game scores only settled markets.
  • 3: 0.52 < 0.55 − 0.02 = 0.53, so Sharp. But with 12 forecasts the noise (about 0.06 per mean) is larger than the 0.03 gap. Do not trust it yet.
  • 4: almost nothing. The interval includes 0.75 (well calibrated) and 0.50 (overconfident). Gather more forecasts.

Summary

The game scores paper forecasts with the Brier score (sum over all states, 0–2) and the log score, both lower-is- better and both proper: honesty minimises your expected score. The calibration chart and the tiers need many forecasts before they mean anything. Forecast skill is separate from trading profit.

Next lesson

Chapter VI.4: from belief to stake. How much should you risk?

Chapter VI.4 — Sizing the Stake: Kelly as a ceiling, risk as a discipline

Learning objectives

  • Compute the Kelly fraction for a $1 claim, and use fractional Kelly only as an upper bound.
  • Combine Kelly with slippage, and see why liquidity usually binds first.
  • Set per-market and total exposure limits, and never go all-in.

Prerequisites

Chapters VI.1–VI.3.

Explanation

The Kelly criterion gives the fraction of your bankroll that maximises long-run growth if your probability is exactly right. For buying a $1 claim at price p when your belief is q (ignoring fees and slippage):

f* = (q − p) / (1 − p)

Three facts make full Kelly dangerous ([Counsel], widely accepted in forecasting practice):

  1. Your q is an estimate. If it is too high, Kelly over-bets, and over-betting by a factor of two already gives zero long-run growth.
  2. Swings are large even when q is right.
  3. In this game, prices move while you buy, so the real edge shrinks as size grows (Chapter VI.2).

So use fractional Kelly (½ or ¼) as a ceiling, never as a target, and cap it further by liquidity and by fixed exposure limits. Never stake your whole bankroll on one market. Keep cash for entry fees and running costs: your career pays bills too. The economy simulations in docs/V8_SOVEREIGN_STANDARD.md show strategies that ran cash below $100 for many rounds ([Demonstrated] that it happens; the rule is [Counsel]).

The game's own NPC traders obey similar discipline ([Demonstrated], src/exchange/npc.ts): each trades at most a fixed share of its wallet per market (2 %–12 %), and their open cost basis may not exceed 60 % of the wallet.

Illustrated example

Bankroll 1, 000 *  * .Whiteisat * *0.40, and you believe 0.50.

  • f* = (0.50 − 0.40)/(1 − 0.40) = 0.1667, so full Kelly is $167, half Kelly $83 and quarter Kelly $42.
  • Half Kelly in this market: $83 buys 148 shares at an average of $0.551 and pushes the price to 0.696.TheEVatyourbeliefis *  * −8.37**. You paid more per share than you think the share is worth!
  • The liquidity limit: EV peaks at about 45–50 shares, roughly $20–23 (Chapter VI.2).

In a b = 120 market, liquidity binds long before Kelly. The right size here is about $20, or 2 % of the bankroll, not $83 or $167.

Step-by-step reasoning: a sizing routine

  1. Compute f* and halve or quarter it. That is the ceiling.
  2. Find the size at which the marginal price reaches your belief minus the fee. That is the liquidity limit.
  3. Apply your per-market cap, for example 2–5 % of your bankroll ([Counsel]).
  4. Check your total exposure across all open markets, for example at most 25 % ([Counsel]).
  5. Take the smallest of these four numbers.

Common mistakes

  • Doubling up after a loss ("chasing"). The next market is independent of your last result. Your bankroll is smaller, so your size should be too.
  • Treating a closed market as cash. A closed market cannot be traded. Until settlement, the game values it only at its cancellation vector (liquidationValue).
  • Ignoring cancellation risk. If you bought 100 White shares in a fresh match market for 43.66andthegameiscancelled(forexamplebythe400−plyplayinglimit), youreceive * *33.33**.
  • All-in on a "sure thing". In a chess game the favourite at 0.82 still fails nearly one time in five.

Advanced insight

Correlated positions count as one. Positions that depend on the same competitor, say a tournament-winner claim on them and "they win" in two of their featured match markets, rise and fall together. For sizing, add them up as a single exposure. Chapter VI.5 shows how.

Worked example

Bankroll $600. A promotion market (b = 80) shows Yes at $0.30, and you believe 0.40.

  • f* = (0.40 − 0.30)/(0.70) = 0.143. Quarter Kelly is about $21.
  • Liquidity: the marginal price reaches 0.396(yourbeliefminusthe1 * *11.91** in total (average $0.347). Beyond that, extra shares lose EV. 50 shares would cost $18.70 and move Yes to 0.445, withEVdownto+1.30.
  • A per-market cap of 3 % gives $18.
  • The smallest limit is liquidity: buy about 34 shares for $11.91, with EV = 0.40 × $34 − 11.91 =  *  * +1.69** (all computed with the game's functions). Check the live quote before you confirm.

Guided exercise

Bankroll $800. A tournament-winner market (b = 150) lists your favourite at $0.25, and you believe 0.30. (a) Full and quarter Kelly in dollars? (b) Near $0.25, roughly how much does each share move the price? (c) What other check must you do before buying?

Independent exercises

  1. Compute f* for q = 0.55, p = 0.50, and for q = 0.30, p = 0.25.
  2. Why is a quarter-Kelly stake "safer" if your probabilities tend to be overconfident?
  3. You hold positions costing $120, $80 and $60 in three markets on the same competitor, and your bankroll is $1,000. What is your exposure on that competitor as a percentage?
  4. Name two reasons the NPC traders' 60 % exposure cap is higher than a sensible cap for you.

Answers

  • Guided: (a) f* = 0.05/0.75 = 0.0667, so full Kelly ≈ 53 *  * andquarter ≈  * *13. (b) 0.25 × 0.75/150 ≈ 0.00125, about 0.1 cents per share. (c) Total and correlated exposure. Is this competitor already in your other positions?
  • 1: (0.55 − 0.50)/0.50 = 0.10; (0.30 − 0.25)/0.75 = 0.0667.
  • 2: an overconfident q inflates f*. A smaller fraction leaves room for the error, and over-betting harms growth much more than under-betting.
  • 3: $260 out of $1,000 = 26 %, as one correlated exposure.
  • 4: for example: NPC wallets are topped up each season from the treasury (up to $4,000), while your losses are not refunded. NPCs also have no careers, entry fees or club costs to pay. ([Demonstrated] top-up rule; the comparison is [Counsel].)

Summary

Kelly f* = (q − p)/(1 − p) is a ceiling, not a target. Use ½ or ¼ of it at most. In the Crown Exchange, slippage usually limits size first: stop where the marginal price meets your belief minus the fee. Add correlated positions together, cap per-market and total exposure, keep cash for your career, and never go all-in.

Next lesson

Chapter VI.5: forecasting whole tournaments, where outcomes are linked.

Chapter VI.5 — Tournament Forecasting: correlated outcomes and hedging

Learning objectives

  • Know every Exchange market family, its states, and how it closes, settles and cancels.
  • Reason about correlated outcomes across markets.
  • Hedge a position by partial sale and compute the resulting outcomes.

Prerequisites

Chapters VI.1–VI.4; Book V, Chapter V.4 (formats and tiebreaks).

Explanation

Market families. [Demonstrated] src/exchange/families.ts RULES:

Family States Trading closes Settles on Cancellation pays
Match White / Draw / Black the match starts (live: after each published move) the result 1/3 per share
Winner (Swiss Open, Championship) every entrant first round processed or first game started the champion (joint: shares split) 1/n
Promotion Yes / No (top two) last league round starts the promotion list ½
Qualification Yes / No (Crown Championship) last league round starts the Championship field ½
Season title every division member last league round starts the title holder (league order) 1/16
Bracket 8 final-four paths the semifinals start the realised path |S|/8 per share of claim S

The public models use public ratings and recorded results only: the Davidson match model, and Monte Carlo simulations of the remaining league rounds, of Swiss events and of the bracket (src/exchange/families.ts). Markets close when their closing round starts, so no result is ever traded after it is known (src/app/markets.ts).

Correlated outcomes move together. A competitor who wins their games raises their price in every market they appear in at once. Markets on the same competitor, or on competitors in the same league, are linked. In the bracket market, claims are subsets of the same 8 paths, so "champion", "finalist" and "beats Y in the final" are nested. A conjunction claim pays nothing if its condition fails. It is not refunded.

Hedging means reducing the spread of your possible outcomes, usually by selling part of a position after the price has moved. In this game you cannot short, so you hedge by selling what you hold (or, in a multi-state market, by buying other states).

Illustrated example

You bought 100 White shares at 0.40for * *50.78** (fee included). Later, other traders move the market to White $0.60 · Draw $0.20 · Black $0.20. Computed with the game's functions (b = 120):

Choice Cash now If White wins If not
Hold all 100 $0 +$49.22 −$50.78
Sell 50 (nets $27.17, price falls to $0.497) $27.17 +$26.39 −$23.61
Sell all 100 (nets $49.23, price falls to $0.395) $49.23 −$1.55 −$1.55

Selling everything at the new price still loses money: selling 100 shares pushes the price back down (slippage), and you pay the fee twice. Hedging has a price. It is worth paying only if your belief has changed or your exposure is too large.

Step-by-step reasoning: a tournament forecast

  1. Start from the public model, and know what it uses: public ratings and recorded results.
  2. Ask what it cannot know: a high-RD rating is a weak signal (Book V, Chapter V.3), and the remaining schedule matters (who still plays whom).
  3. Write your probability vector as a paper forecast before trading.
  4. Map your exposure: list every market in which this competitor appears.
  5. Trade only the difference between your belief and the price, sized by Chapter VI.4.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking you are diversified when you are not. Three markets on one competitor are one bet.
  • Buying a conjunction expecting a refund. "X beats Y in the final" pays $0 if Y never reaches the final.
  • Trading a winner market you might enter. Your entry cancels it at 1/n, so your position returns 1/n per share, whatever you paid.
  • Forgetting the conflict rule. If you sponsor a competitor, the game refuses your buy orders in their markets.

Advanced insight

In the bracket market every claim is priced from the same 8 path prices, so you can check coherence yourself: the champion claim must equal the sum of its two paths, and the finalist claim the sum of its four. If you believe one path is mispriced, the cheapest way to act is the narrowest claim containing it. Broader claims carry the other paths' prices too ([Counsel], following directly from the [Demonstrated] claim structure).

Worked example

A 16-player division title market. The public model gives the leader 0.35 with four rounds to go. The leader's remaining opponents are the three strongest players in the division, so you estimate 0.28. The leader's price is $0.34. Do not buy the leader, and do not "short" it either (impossible). Your options are a paper forecast of 0.28, or buying a rival you think is underpriced, if your belief about that rival is also above its price. A low opinion of one competitor does not by itself make any other one cheap.

Guided exercise

In a fresh bracket market (all 8 paths at $0.125), what does a "champion" claim cost? A "finalist" claim? If you buy 10 champion shares for competitor A, how does the price of A's finalist claim change, and why?

Independent exercises

  1. Using the illustrated example, what is your profit if you sell 50 shares and White then draws?
  2. Why do promotion and qualification markets pay ½ per share on cancellation, while season title markets pay 1/16?
  3. You hold X in the Federation Open winner market and then buy "X wins" in a featured match market of one of X's Open games. Are these positions correlated? In which direction?
  4. Why can no result be traded after it is known in the Exchange?

Answers

  • Guided: champion = 2 paths = 0.25 * *;finalist = 4paths =  * *0.50. Buying A's champion claim adds shares to A's two champion paths, which are also two of A's four finalist paths. So A's finalist price rises too. One inventory keeps the prices coherent.
  • 1: a draw is "not White": −$23.61.
  • 2: cancellation pays the uniform vector 1/n: two states give ½, sixteen states give 1/16.
  • 3: yes, positively. Winning that game raises X's chance of winning the Open, so both positions gain together, and losing it hurts both. Count them as one exposure.
  • 4: markets close when their closing round starts, and match markets close at the final move. Live trading happens only between published moves, and quotes taken before a move are rejected after it.

Summary

Know each family's states, closing time, settlement and cancellation. Public models use only public information. Linked markets are one exposure. Hedge by selling what you hold, but remember that slippage and fees make hedging costly. Trade only the gap between a written belief and the price.

Next lesson

Chapter VI.6: forecasting a game while it is being played.

Chapter VI.6 — Live Odds and the Uncertain Board

Learning objectives

  • Know exactly how in-play trading works and what information is public.
  • Compute the game's live model from an engine evaluation.
  • Judge how certain a chess position really is, and what that means for a forecast.

Prerequisites

Book V, Chapter V.6 (the expected-score scale); Chapters VI.1–VI.5.

Explanation

In-play trading. [Demonstrated] src/app/federation.ts, src/ui/SpectatorScreen.tsx. When you watch a featured Federation game live, its match market can be traded between moves. After each move is published, then before the next move is computed, you see what every trader sees: the moves, the engine's own evaluation, and the price history. Future moves do not exist while you can trade. Each move is computed only after the trading window closes, and a trade queued while a move is being computed is rejected once it is published. Move grades stay hidden until the market is settled or cancelled, and Match Analysis runs only then.

The live model (crown-odds-2) [Demonstrated] src/exchange/odds.ts, docs/ODDS_MODEL.md. It is a forecast, never the price. It is an ordered logit: one latent number x measures White's advantage, a draw width θ ≥ 0 sits on both sides of it, and with σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^−z):

P(White) = σ(x − θ), P(Black) = σ(−x − θ), P(Draw) = 1 − P(White) − P(Black).

Before the game, x comes from the public rating gap (deflated by both RDs, as in Glicko) plus a small fitted first-move edge for White, and θ from the players' level (stronger pairs draw more). After each published move n, with the published evaluation e (White's view, in units of 100 cp, clamped at ±16):

x = a(n)·x₀ + b(n)·e, θ = θ₀ · exp(d(n) + m·(material traded)).

a, b and d were fitted on 3,200 Federation-style engine games (held-out validated; the report is in docs/ODDS_MODEL.md). The rating prior keeps a decaying weight: a = 0.83 at ply 10, 0.59 at ply 40, 0.15 at ply 160. The evaluation's weight b rises to a peak near ply 40. The draw width grows with the ply count and with traded material, because long, simplified games are drawish. At ply 0 the live model is exactly the pre-game forecast.

Two NPC desks act in-play: Kestrel Tactical Desk trades on this model, and Tidewater Momentum buys whatever has risen since the last window (price history only).

A fact worth noticing. [Demonstrated] Up to v0.8 the live model used only the evaluation, so at 0 cp it gave about 0.35 / 0.30 / 0.35 whatever the ratings (bug #21 in docs/BUG_REGISTER.md). crown-odds-2 fixed this: at an equal evaluation the favourite stays the favourite, by a margin that fades as the game goes on. How much the ratings should still count late in a game is where your own judgement as a forecaster comes in.

Illustrated example

A featured game between public ratings 1850 (White) and 1750, both RD 70. Pre-game model: 0.660 / 0.107 / 0.233. Live model after ply 20 with all pieces still on the board, computed with the game's own liveWdl, next to an equal pairing (1800 v 1800) for comparison:

Evaluation (White) 1850 v 1750: W / D / B 1800 v 1800: W / D / B
0 cp 0.578 / 0.172 / 0.251 0.462 / 0.190 / 0.347
+50 cp 0.690 / 0.139 / 0.170 0.584 / 0.170 / 0.246
+150 cp 0.855 / 0.073 / 0.072 0.788 / 0.102 / 0.109
+300 cp 0.962 / 0.020 / 0.018 0.942 / 0.031 / 0.028
−150 cp 0.240 / 0.168 / 0.592 0.166 / 0.137 / 0.697

And the same 1850 v 1750 game at a level 0 cp as the ply count grows (all pieces on): ply 1 0.662 / 0.107 / 0.231, ply 10 0.613 / 0.133 / 0.253, ply 40 0.495 / 0.259 / 0.246, ply 80 0.341 / 0.447 / 0.212, ply 160 0.230 / 0.587 / 0.184. A level position late in the game is mostly a draw.

Step-by-step reasoning: how certain is this board?

An evaluation is an estimate from a search of limited depth, and its certainty varies a lot.

  1. Forced mate on the board: the result is settled (the first board is proven by exhaustive search). A forecast should be near 1, and only the remaining time on the clock adds doubt.
  2. A large but unforced edge (+300 cp): the map says about 0.93 in engine games. But the map was fitted on engine games, and a weaker or time-pressed player converts less reliably ([Counsel]).
  3. A balanced position (the second board): the evaluation says little. The draw rate and the players' strengths dominate, which is why the live model keeps a share of the rating prior and widens the draw band as the game goes on.
  4. Volatile positions: if the evaluation has swung several times, the search is struggling. Widen your uncertainty rather than chasing each swing ([Counsel]).

Common mistakes

  • Treating the evaluation as the probability. It is an input to a model that maps it to an expected score.
  • Chasing momentum. A price that rose in the last window carries no promise about the next one.
  • Trading on a stale quote. It will be rejected. Read the new position first.
  • Expecting grades during the game. They appear only after settlement.

Advanced insight

The logistic σ is steep near balance and flat near decisive positions, like the map of Book V, Chapter V.6. So a 100 cp swing around 0 moves the live model much more than a 100 cp swing around +500. When a featured game is balanced, small evaluation changes produce large live-model changes, and prices driven by the Tactical Desk can swing. That is where a forecaster who reads the position calmly can disagree most usefully ([Counsel]).

Worked example

The 1850 v 1750 game above. After move 18 (ply 36) the evaluation is +150 cp for White, and one rook pair has been exchanged (material 40 of 50). The live model says 0.852 / 0.098 / 0.050. The price of White is $0.80. You have watched the game: White's advantage is a protected passed pawn, and Black has no counterplay. You believe 0.88.

  • Small-trade break-even: 1.01 × 0.80 = 0.808 < 0.88, so the trade is in your favour.
  • Size it with Chapter VI.4: a match market has b = 120, so at $0.80 each share moves the price about 0.80 × 0.20/120 ≈ 0.0013. Stop well before the price reaches about 0.87.
  • Write the paper forecast as well. It is scored even if you do not trade.

Guided exercise

The model's latent advantage is x = 0.8 and the draw width θ = 0.5. Compute W, D and B, and check that they add up to 1 (σ(0.3) ≈ 0.574, σ(−1.3) ≈ 0.214).

Independent exercises

  1. With x = 0 and θ = 0.26, what are W, D and B? What happens to D when θ grows?
  2. Why does the game reject a trade that you queued while the next move was being computed?
  3. Name the two NPC traders that act in-play and the information each one uses.
  4. Why is a featured game that is stopped by the playing-length limit cancelled rather than settled as a draw?

Answers

  • Guided: W = σ(0.8 − 0.5) = σ(0.3) ≈ 0.574, B = σ(−0.8 − 0.5) = σ(−1.3) ≈ 0.214, D = 1 − 0.574 − 0.214 = 0.211 (rounded figures; the three add up to 1 by construction). The published vector also floors each state at 0.005 and renormalises, which matters only near certainty.
  • 1: W = B = σ(−0.26) ≈ 0.435, D ≈ 0.129. A larger θ pushes both σ terms down, so D grows: θ is the width of the draw band.
  • 2: the market's revision changes when a move is published. A quote taken before new public information can never execute after it.
  • 3: Kestrel Tactical Desk (the public engine evaluation of the current position, through the live model) and Tidewater Momentum (price history only). The fans and novices also trade live, on the live model plus their noise and bias.
  • 4: a game stopped by the limit has no real result. It is censored. The market pays its published cancellation vector (1/3), and the standings record an adjudicated draw, labelled as such.

Summary

Live trading happens between published moves, on public information only. Grades stay hidden until settlement. The live model (crown-odds-2) combines a fading share of the rating gap with the evaluation through an ordered logit, with a draw band that widens in long and simplified games. Judge how certain the board really is: proven mate, large edge, balanced, volatile.

Chapter VI.7: the other traders, your own biases, and the long run.

Chapter VI.7 — The Crowd and the Mirror: NPC traders, overconfidence and the long run

Learning objectives

  • Describe the NPC traders exactly as the code defines them.
  • Recognise overconfidence and the other common forecasting and trading errors.
  • Separate luck from skill with sample sizes.

Prerequisites

All earlier chapters of Book VI.

Explanation

The NPC traders (crown-npc-traders-2). [Demonstrated] src/exchange/npc.ts. All eight trade through the same LMSR as you, long-only, with funded wallets. They use only information available when they decide: the published model (public ratings), the live engine evaluation during play, and public price history. They never see hidden strength or any future move or result. No trader is guaranteed to profit.

Trader Behaviour Noise Margin Budget per market Acts
Old Harbour Fund conservative value; trades only large mispricings 0.05 0.06 2 % pre-game, between rounds
Crown Supporters Club overconfident fans of the favourite (+0.06 on the favourite) 0.08 0.02 5 % pre-game, live
Lantern Contrarians back the underdog (+0.06) 0.08 0.04 3 % pre-game, between rounds
First-Time Forecasters noisy novices 0.14 0.02 3 % pre-game, live
Tidewater Momentum buys what has risen since the last window — 0.03 2 % live, between rounds
Summit Tournament Partners tournament specialist (season and tournament markets) 0.03 0.02 6 % pre-game, between rounds
Kestrel Tactical Desk trades in-play on the public evaluation 0.03 0.03 4 % live
Meridian Analytics calibrated fundamental trader on the public model 0.03 0.02 12 % pre-game, between rounds

Noise is the standard deviation added to the public belief, and margin is the minimum edge a value trader demands. A value trader buys the claim with the largest (belief − price − margin) up to a target price of (belief − margin). Biased and noisy traders act first and the informed ones last, so prices usually end near the public consensus, with residual noise. Wallets are topped up each season to at most $4,000, and open exposure is capped at 60 % of the wallet.

What this means for you ([Counsel], reasoned from the [Demonstrated] design): the price you see usually reflects the public model closely. If you have an edge at all, it comes from better judgement than the public ratings contain: about rating reliability (RD), about the remaining schedule, and about what the board shows in live games. It does not come from tricks. If you have no view, do not trade. A paper forecast is free.

Illustrated example: overconfidence

A forecaster says 0.9 to every "favourite wins" question. The favourites truly win 70 % of the time. Expected Brier (two-state, game formula): honest 0.70 gives 0.42, while the overconfident 0.90 gives 0.50. In trading, overconfidence makes Kelly-sized stakes far too large, and in this game it also makes you push prices past your true break-even (Chapter VI.4).

Step-by-step reasoning: luck versus skill

Suppose every trade is like the Chapter VI.2 example: 50 shares bought at 0.40for * *22.78**, in an outcome that is truly 50 %. EV = +$2.22 per trade. The outcome alone has a standard deviation of $25 per trade. With independent trades (computed with a normal approximation):

Trades Expected profit Standard deviation Chance of being behind anyway
1 $2 $25 46.5 %
10 $22 $79 38.9 %
100 $222 $250 18.7 %
400 $889 $500 3.8 %
1,000 $2,222 $791 0.2 %

A genuine edge can lose for a long time, and a bad trader can be ahead after ten trades. Results tell you about skill only over hundreds of comparable decisions. Your Brier score against the public forecast is usually a faster, cleaner signal than your profit.

Common mistakes

  1. Outcome bias: "I lost, so it was a bad trade." Judge EV at the time of the trade.
  2. Overconfidence: probabilities too close to 0 or 1.
  3. Anchoring on the price: write your belief first.
  4. Chasing losses, or doubling up after a win.
  5. Ignoring the fee and slippage, especially on round trips.
  6. Mistaking correlation for diversification.
  7. Trading without a view: when you have no view, the fee is your only certainty.
  8. Letting the Exchange take over your career. Forecasting skill is not chess skill, and cash lost on the Exchange is cash you no longer have for entry fees and club costs.

Advanced insight

Base rates first. Before any specific reasoning, start from the base rate (for example the ≈ 31 % draw rate between equals in the result model), then adjust for specifics. Forecasters who start from the specifics tend to overreact to vivid details such as a dramatic last game ([Counsel], a well-established finding in forecasting practice, not measured in this game).

Worked example: a forecaster's journal entry

Market: season title, 4 rounds left. Price of competitor K: $0.22. Public model: 0.24. My belief: 0.30. Reason: K's rating is provisional (RD 180) after a strong run of results. I think K is better than the rating says, and K's remaining opponents are the weakest four. Exposure on K elsewhere: none. Size: quarter Kelly = (0.30 − 0.22)/0.78/4 ≈ 2.6 % of the bankroll, capped to 2 %. Paper forecast: recorded. Review date: after settlement. Check the Brier score and whether the provisional rating moved the way I expected.

Guided exercise

A trader tells you: "I've made money on 7 of my last 10 trades, so I'm skilled." Using the table, write two questions you would ask before agreeing.

Independent exercises

  1. Which NPC trader would you expect to buy the favourite in a pre-game match market, even when the price already matches the public model? Why?
  2. Can any NPC trader see a competitor's hidden strength? Quote the rule.
  3. Your mean Brier is 0.55 over 200 forecasts, and the public forecast's is 0.58 on the same markets. Is that stronger evidence of skill than a $300 profit over 30 trades? Explain.
  4. Give one reason why the order in which NPC traders act matters for the price you see.

Answers

  • Guided: for example: What was the expected value of those trades at the time? How large were they, and how many would it take to separate luck from skill? (Ten trades leave a 39 % chance of being behind with a real edge, so a lucky player can easily be ahead.)
  • 1: Crown Supporters Club: its belief adds +0.06 to the favourite, and its margin is only 0.02.
  • 2: no. "Information available at decision time only: the published model (public ratings), the board position's public engine evaluation during live play, and public price history — never hidden strength, never a future move or result." The competitor model also notes that hidden strength is "never used by forecasts or NPC traders".
  • 3: yes, very likely. Over 200 forecasts the noise in a mean Brier is roughly 0.014, so a 0.03 gap is about two standard deviations. A $300 profit over 30 trades can easily come from luck (see the table).
  • 4: the biased and noisy traders act first and the informed ones last, so the informed traders correct much of the noise and the final price ends near the public consensus.

Summary

The NPC traders trade on public information only, with documented biases, noise and limits, and no one is guaranteed a profit. Prices therefore tend to sit near the public model. Any edge you have must come from better judgement, and a paper forecast is the free way to test it. Beware overconfidence, outcome bias and correlation. Skill shows only over large samples, and the Brier score shows it faster than profit.
