The Twelve-Week Program (docs/grimoire/07-twelve-week-program.md) puts Books I–VI into a schedule, and the Glossary (docs/grimoire/08-glossary.md) defines every term used in them.

The Twelve-Week Program — From Apprentice to Sovereign

A training schedule for Crown & Calculation that uses Books I–VI, the Academy, the Lab and the Federation.

This program turns the six books into twelve weeks of practice. Each week has the same parts: objective, reading, Academy work, practice games, skills to demonstrate, review questions and a progress check. Three adjustments (Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced) and four daily lengths (10, 20, 30 and 60 minutes) let you fit it to your level and your time.

How the program uses the game

[Demonstrated] All of the following come from the game's code (src/academy/*, src/ui/AcademyScreen.tsx, src/engine/levels.ts, src/games/types.ts):

  • Academy modes: Tactical Academy (themed puzzles; choose a theme button, or let difficulty adapt), Puzzle Rush (3 minutes, three strikes; any solve with a hint or a wrong move counts as a strike), Calculation Chamber (puzzles needing two or more of your moves; 72 in the practice pool), Defensive Survival (251), Endgame Workshop (116; solve, then play the position out against the engine), Replay Your Mistakes (moves from your analysed games that lost ≥ 0.12 expected score), Adaptive Training (your weakest themes) and Held-out Assessment (10 puzzles you have never seen).
  • Puzzle pools by theme (practice split, retired puzzles excluded): Defensive resource 173, Endgame technique 116, Hanging piece 109, Calculation 83, Position evaluation 76, Fork 44, Skewer 34, Pin 30, Discovered attack 13, Promotion race 10, Mate threat 9, Checkmate 1. A puzzle can carry several themes.
  • Assessments are a scarce resource. There are 81 held-out puzzles, and each is shown at most once, so you have about eight ten-puzzle assessments in total. This program uses four: weeks 1, 4, 8 and 12. Do not spend them casually. Each one is a measurement, not training.
  • Opponents: engine levels L1 Novice (800) to L8 Crown (2926) and L9 Sovereign Unbound (3038, derived), plus Federation competitors via Random Federation Quick Match or your league fixtures. These ratings are on the Crown scale, not FIDE.
  • Time controls: Blitz 3+2, Rapid 5+3 (used for Federation games), Classical 15+10, Untimed. Untimed games are never rated. Each timed control has its own rating pool.
  • Review: Analysis (Quick, Standard and Deep presets), Retry from This Position (Unrated), bookmarks, the Lab (with 95 % intervals and "insufficient evidence" flags) and Paper Forecasts with Brier scoring.

Keep one analysis preset (Standard) for your record. The Lab combines only reports of one methodology (Book V, Chapter V.6).

Level adjustments

Beginner Intermediate Advanced
Who new to chess, or rated below about 1200 (Crown) about 1200–1900 about 1900 and above
Main opponents L1–L3 L3–L5, Federation 1300–1900 L5–L8, Federation 1900+
Main time control Untimed, then Rapid 5+3 Rapid 5+3, Classical 15+10 Classical 15+10, Rapid 5+3
Puzzle difficulty let the Academy adapt from 1–2 adapt from 2–3 adapt from 3–5
Reading every chapter fully, all exercises skim chapters you know; do every exercise read Books V–VI fully; Books I–IV only for review
Book VI strand paper forecasts only, no trading paper forecasts; small trades (≤ 2 % of cash) from week 8 full strand, sized by Book VI, Chapter VI.4

Daily session variants

Pick the length you can keep up every day. Consistency beats length ([Counsel]).

Daily time Shape of a session
10 minutes 5 themed puzzles in the week's theme, or one Puzzle Rush, then 2 minutes rereading one Summary section. Play one game per week at the weekend.
20 minutes 10 themed puzzles + one Rush; or one Rapid 5+3 game with a 5-minute review of its first turning point.
30 minutes 10 puzzles (week theme) + one Rapid game + a review using Retry from This Position on your worst move.
60 minutes 15 minutes reading and exercises, 15 minutes Academy (week theme + one Rush), one Classical 15+10 or two Rapid games, 10 minutes Analysis review, and one paper forecast.

The weekly targets below assume the 30-minute session. With 10 minutes, halve the puzzle and game counts. With 60 minutes, use the upper numbers.

Week 1 — The Rules and the Board

  • Objective: play legal, complete games without hesitation, and know every Crown rule that differs from orthodox chess.
  • Read: Book I, Chapters 1–3 (The Board and Its Coordinates; The Pieces I: Rook, Queen and King; The Pieces II: Knight and Pawn) and Chapter 7 (Stalemate and the Other Draws). Rulebook §§3–5 and §10.
  • Academy: take Assessment 1 (baseline: 10 held-out puzzles; write down your score). Then 20 Tactical Academy puzzles at the adaptive difficulty.
  • Practice games: 5 Untimed games against L1 (Beginner), L2 (Intermediate) or L4 (Advanced). Every game ends in checkmate, a draw rule or resignation. Note which rule ended it.
  • Demonstrate: no illegal-move attempts; correctly predict when a position is bare kings, stalemate or a claimable threefold repetition.
  • Review questions: (1) Why is there no double pawn step or en passant? (2) Which draws are automatic, and which must be claimed? (3) If you flag on time while your opponent has a single pawn left, what is the result?
  • Progress check: a written baseline: Assessment 1 score, and your first five game results by termination type.

Week 2 — Piece Safety and Basic Tactics

  • Objective: stop losing pieces for nothing, and win the ones your opponent leaves hanging.
  • Read: Book I, Chapter 4 (Capturing and Piece Safety) and Chapter 5 (Check and Escaping Check). Book II, The Duellist: its chapters on double attacks, forks and pins.
  • Academy: 40 puzzles: Hanging piece (20), Fork (10), Pin (10). Two Puzzle Rush runs (record the best).
  • Practice games: 5 Rapid 5+3 games: L2 (Beginner), L3–L4 (Intermediate), L5 (Advanced). Analyse each game with Standard.
  • Demonstrate: no Blunder grades caused by a hanging piece in your last three games. Use the coach's Hanging pieces topic as the check.
  • Review questions: (1) What three questions do you ask before every move? (2) Why are knight forks especially common on a 6×6 board? (3) What does the coach mean by "threat awareness"?
  • Progress check: Rush best score compared with week 1, and the number of hanging-piece notes per game.

Week 3 — Checkmates and Defence

  • Objective: deliver the basic mates quickly, and survive attacks by finding the only move.
  • Read: Book I, Chapter 6 (Checkmate: King and Queen, King and Rook) and Chapter 8 (Simple Winning Patterns). Book II: its chapters on mating patterns and defence. Book V, Chapter V.5 (Critical Moments, Stronger Opponents and Predictable Mistakes), "Explanation" section only.
  • Academy: 30 Defensive Survival puzzles; all 9 Mate threat puzzles; the Grimoire's mate-in-1 and mate-in-2 boards in Book I. (The Academy's Checkmate pool has only one puzzle; the Grimoire boards are exhaustively verified substitutes.)
  • Practice games: 4 Rapid games; in two of them, start a training game from a position where you have K+Q or K+R against K and mate within 20 moves (Untimed).
  • Demonstrate: K+Q vs K and K+R vs K mates from any start position; one game saved with a defensive only-move.
  • Review questions: (1) Why is the sixth rank (first rank for White) a mating wall? (2) How does a stalemate trap arise when you are mating with K+Q? (3) What is a "critical moment" in the game's Analysis?
  • Progress check: your Defensive Survival first-try clean rate (Academy statistics) with its sample size.

Week 4 — Combinations

  • Objective: chain two or three forcing moves into a combination, and verify it before playing it.
  • Read: Book II's chapters on combinations, discovered attacks and skewers. Book V, Chapter V.1 (The Pruned Tree: calculation and candidate discipline), complete with exercises.
  • Academy: 15 Calculation Chamber puzzles; Skewer (10) and Discovered attack (all 13). Then take Assessment 2.
  • Practice games: 4 Rapid games against an opponent 100–200 points above you (a level or a Federation competitor).
  • Demonstrate: solve Book V's exercises V.1.1–V.1.3 without hints; in a game, play one combination that you had calculated to the end.
  • Review questions: (1) Why do you need only one good defence to reject a candidate, but must refute every defence to accept one? (2) Why is the quiet move Rb5 in Book V's worked example easy to miss? (3) Did your Assessment 2 score change from Assessment 1, and is a ten-puzzle difference meaningful?
  • Progress check: Assessment 2 compared with Assessment 1. Remember that 10 puzzles is a small sample. The Lab combines all assessments and shows the uncertainty.

Week 5 — Openings

  • Objective: have a small, sound repertoire as White and a reply to each of White's ten first moves as Black.
  • Read: Book III, The Strategist: its opening-principles chapter. Book V, Chapter V.7 (The Sixty-Four Gates: building a repertoire). Book VI, Chapter VI.1 (The Language of Chance).
  • Academy: 20 puzzles of your choice, plus Adaptive Training (10).
  • Practice games: 6 Rapid games, three as White with your chosen first move, and three as Black with your prepared replies. Opponents: L3 (Beginner), L5 (Intermediate), L6–L7 (Advanced).
  • Oracle strand: record 3 paper forecasts on featured match markets (Book VI, VI.1).
  • Demonstrate: a one-sentence plan for each of your repertoire lines; no opening-phase Mistake in three games.
  • Review questions: (1) What does "balanced" mean for the 64 book openings? (2) Why is memorising beyond move 3 of little use here? (3) What is the implied probability of a $0.31 Draw price?
  • Progress check: the Lab's Opening understanding rate (or "insufficient evidence"; it needs at least 10 opportunities from 3 games).

Week 6 — Pawn Structure

  • Objective: read pawn structures and play for the faster majority.
  • Read: Book III's chapters on pawn structure, passed pawns and weak squares. Book I, Chapter 9 (The Pawn's Road: Four Steps to the Crown). Book V, Chapter V.2 (Complexity, Imbalance and the Art of Simplifying).
  • Academy: all 10 Promotion race puzzles; Position evaluation (15).
  • Practice games: 4 Rapid or 2 Classical games. In each, write at move 12 which side has the faster pawn majority, and check your note against the evaluation graph afterwards.
  • Oracle strand: 3 more paper forecasts. Read Book VI, Chapter VI.2 (The Engine of Prices).
  • Demonstrate: win or hold one game by pawn play; solve Book V exercises V.2.1–V.2.2.
  • Review questions: (1) Why are passed pawns more dangerous on 6×6 than on 8×8? (2) When should you trade into a pawn ending? (3) How much does the price move when you buy 30 shares in a fresh match market?
  • Progress check: your Promotion-race solve rate and the coach's Promotion races note count per game.

Week 7 — Endgames

  • Objective: convert won endings and hold drawn ones, with the Crown draw and timeout rules in mind.
  • Read: Book IV, The Master: its endgame chapters. Rulebook §10 (draws) and §13 (clocks).
  • Academy: 25 Endgame Workshop puzzles. For five of them, use play out against the engine after solving.
  • Practice games: 4 Rapid games. In two of them, use Retry from This Position (Unrated) from an endgame you mishandled.
  • Oracle strand: 3 paper forecasts; read Book VI, Chapter VI.3 (Measuring the Oracle).
  • Demonstrate: convert one winning ending against L4+; hold one inferior ending to a draw (repetition, bare kings or stalemate).
  • Review questions: (1) What happens on time-out when your opponent has only a king? (2) When is a 100-halfmove draw automatic, and when must it be claimed? (3) Compute the Brier score of a forecast (0.5, 0.3, 0.2) that ends in a draw.
  • Progress check: the Lab's Endgame technique rate with its interval.

Week 8 — Calculation

  • Objective: calculate forcing lines three moves deep, accurately and in reasonable time.
  • Read: Book V, Chapter V.1 again (redo the guided exercise from memory) and Chapter V.5. Book VI, Chapter VI.4 (Sizing the Stake).
  • Academy: 25 Calculation Chamber puzzles; 3 Puzzle Rush runs. Then take Assessment 3.
  • Practice games: 3 Classical 15+10 games. Before each critical-looking move, write your candidate list with one named refutation each.
  • Oracle strand: Intermediate and Advanced may start small trades (Intermediate ≤ 2 % of cash per market). Beginners keep to paper forecasts.
  • Demonstrate: in a Classical game, a correct three-move forcing line. Assessment 3 completed.
  • Review questions: (1) In what order do you list candidates? (2) What is the Kelly fraction for q = 0.5, p = 0.4, and why is half of it still too much in a b = 120 market? (3) Did your clean rate in the Calculation Chamber rise compared with week 4?
  • Progress check: Assessment 3 compared with Assessments 1–2; the Lab's Calculation dimension.

Week 9 — Positional Play and Defence

  • Objective: make good quiet moves, and defend worse positions patiently.
  • Read: Book III's chapters on planning and piece activity. Book IV's chapter on defence. Book V, Chapter V.3 (Reading the Opponent: profiling and style adaptation).
  • Academy: 20 Position evaluation puzzles; 20 Defensive Survival puzzles; Adaptive Training (10).
  • Practice games: 4 games against Federation competitors (Quick Match or league fixtures). Before each, write a profile: rating, RD, style (is it validated?), and your plan.
  • Oracle strand: 3 paper forecasts on Federation markets; read Book VI, Chapter VI.5 (Tournament Forecasting).
  • Demonstrate: one game with no Mistake in its quiet (non-critical) moves; a written opponent profile that correctly states which styles affect play.
  • Review questions: (1) Which four styles are validated, and what does each change? (2) What does a high RD tell you about a rating? (3) Why are three markets on one competitor a single exposure?
  • Progress check: the Lab's Positional understanding and Defensive awareness rates.

Week 10 — Tournaments and Time

  • Objective: manage the clock and the standings across an event.
  • Read: Book V, Chapter V.4 (The Tournament Hall: Swiss, leagues and knockouts). Rulebook §§16–17. Book VI, Chapter VI.6 (Live Odds and the Uncertain Board).
  • Academy: 3 Puzzle Rush runs (speed under pressure); 15 mixed puzzles.
  • Practice games: play the league/Swiss rounds that fall in your season, or simulate a 5-round Swiss: five Rapid 5+3 games against opponents within ±150 of you. Add 3 Blitz 3+2 games to practise knockout tie-breaks.
  • Oracle strand: watch one featured game live. Write a paper forecast before the game and a second one at move 20, and compare both with the live model (Book VI, VI.6).
  • Demonstrate: no time forfeits; compute your event performance rating and check it against the Squire norm.
  • Review questions: (1) What is the Swiss tiebreak order? (2) How is a level knockout match resolved, and what changes in the final? (3) At an evaluation of +150 cp, what does the live model give?
  • Progress check: the Lab's Time management dimension; your performance rating for the event.

Week 11 — Engine Analysis and Preparation

  • Objective: turn every loss into training, and prepare for specific opponents.
  • Read: Book V, Chapter V.6 (The Engine's Mirror) and Chapter V.8 (The Unbound Challenge). Book VI, Chapter VI.7 (The Crowd and the Mirror).
  • Academy: Replay Your Mistakes: every puzzle it offers. Then 15 Adaptive Training puzzles.
  • Practice games: 4 games against L7 (Advanced: L8), Classical or Rapid. Analyse each one with the full loss routine from Chapter V.6, and use Retry from This Position (Unrated) at the first turning point.
  • Oracle strand: review all your scored forecasts. Which tier does the game show, and how many forecasts is it based on?
  • Demonstrate: for two losses, a written explanation in words of the better move at the first turning point.
  • Review questions: (1) Convert +100 cp and −200 cp into expected scores. (2) Why are Brilliant labels and Played Like not to be trusted yet? (3) What does a 3.8 % chance of being behind after 400 good trades tell you about short-term results?
  • Progress check: count recurring patterns (5 occurrences in 3 games) and check that each one has assigned training.

Week 12 — Review and the Sovereign Challenge

  • Objective: measure your progress honestly, and challenge Sovereign Unbound with realistic goals.
  • Read: the Summary section of every chapter in Books V and VI. Book V, Chapter V.8 again.
  • Academy: Assessment 4. Then one Rush and 10 Adaptive Training puzzles.
  • Practice games: 2 casual games against L9 at the Fast (1 s) budget to learn it, then 2 rated games against L9 (always 10 s per move) at Classical 15+10. Beginners: replace L9 with the strongest level against which you scored at least 25 % this program, and play L9 only casually.
  • Oracle strand: write a final forecasting review: number of forecasts, mean Brier against the public forecast, and the calibration bins with their intervals.
  • Demonstrate: survive the opening and the first critical moment against L9 in at least one game. (A draw is a triumph: the calibration model gives a 2000-rated player about 0.25 % expected score per game against it.)
  • Review questions: (1) What do the budgets 1/5/10/15/30/60 s mean, and how does the clock limit them? (2) How was L9's 3038 rating obtained, and what does its RD of 171 mean? (3) Compare Assessments 1–4. What changed, and how sure can you be?
  • Progress check (final): see below.

Final progress assessment

Fill in this table at the end of week 12. Every row has a source in the game, so no number has to be guessed.

Measure Week 1 Week 12 Source
Held-out assessment score (of 10) Academy (Assessments 1 and 4)
Puzzle Rush best Academy statistics
First-try clean rate (with n) Academy statistics
Rapid rating (state whether provisional) Passport; provisional while games < 20 or RD > 100
Lab: Tactical vision, Calculation, Endgame technique (rate and 95 % interval) Lab

How to read it ([Counsel]): look for changes larger than the intervals. Ten-puzzle assessments and fewer than 50 forecasts are noisy. If a measure did not move, choose that topic's week and repeat it, before you move on to the next cycle. The program is meant to be run more than once, at a higher level each time.

Glossary of the Grimoire

Terms are defined as Crown & Calculation uses them (variant crown-la6-v1, Federation crown-federation-1, Exchange crown-exchange-2). Where a term means something different in orthodox chess or in real-world markets, the entry says so. Pointers: RB §n = docs/RULEBOOK.md section n; I.n = Book I, Chapter n; V.n / VI.n = Book V or VI, Chapter n; P-Wk n = Twelve-Week Program, week n.

100-halfmove rule. If 100 consecutive halfmoves (50 by each side) pass without a capture or a pawn move, either player may claim a draw. At 150 halfmoves the draw is automatic. → RB §10; I.7.

Accuracy. 100·exp(−4 × mean expected-score loss) over a player's graded moves (crown-accuracy-v2), always between 0 and 100. The constant 4 is an uncalibrated placeholder, so accuracy is labelled experimental. → V.6.

Adaptive Training. Academy mode that picks puzzles from the themes where your first-try record is weakest, or from repeated engine-verified errors in your games. → P-Wk 5.

Agreement, draw by. A draw both players accept. Allowed only after each side has made at least ten moves. → RB §10.

Analysis presets. Quick (depth 5), Standard (depth 7, default) and Deep (depth 9, four candidate lines). The Lab combines only reports of one preset and methodology. → V.6.

Assessment (Held-out Assessment). Ten puzzles from the 81-puzzle held-out split, each shown to a player at most once and never used in practice. It measures; it does not train. → V.6; P-Wk 1.

b (liquidity parameter). The LMSR constant that sets how far prices move per share: match markets 120, tournament winner 150, promotion and qualification 80, season title and bracket 100, Sandbox 60. → VI.2.

Bare kings. Only the two kings remain. This is an automatic draw, the only insufficient-material case drawn automatically in Crown. → RB §10; V.5.

Blitz / Rapid / Classical / Untimed. Time controls 3+2, 5+3, 15+10 (minutes + seconds per move) and none. Each timed control has its own rating pool. Untimed games are never rated. Federation games use Rapid 5+3. → RB §13.

Bookmark / Memorable move. Analysis markers that save a ply of a game for later study. → V.6.

Bounded selection. How engine levels L1–L4 choose: at random (softmax with a temperature) among the moves whose score is within a fixed margin of their own best (L1 320 cp … L4 70 cp). It is never used when a mate is found. → V.3.

Bracket market. An Exchange family over the 8 possible final-four paths of the Crown Championship. Claims (champion, finalist, "X beats Y in the final") are sets of paths. A conjunction claim pays $0 if its condition fails. → VI.5.

Brier score. The game's forecast score: B = Σ over all states of (p − y)², from 0 (perfect) to 2 (worst); lower is better. For a two-state market this is twice the usual binary Brier. → VI.3.

Brilliant / Great. Special grades for a best move that is clearly better than every alternative (Great), and that also invests verified material (Brilliant). Not validated; Brilliant-move achievements wait for validated grading. → V.6.

Buchholz / Buchholz Cut-1. Swiss tiebreaks: the sum of your opponents' scores, and that sum minus the lowest one. → V.4; RB §16.

Calculation Chamber. Academy mode with puzzles needing two or more of your own moves against best defence. → V.1.

Calibration. Agreement between stated probabilities and observed frequencies. The game shows ten probability bins, each with a Wilson 95 % interval. (Calibration also names the engine-strength measurement in src/engine/calibration.json.) → VI.3.

Cancellation (market). Resolving a market without a result. Holders receive the published cancellation vector: 1/n per share for most families, |S|/n for a claim on S states, and the opening prices for Sandbox markets. Cancelled markets are not scored as forecasts. → VI.1; RB §20.

Candidate move. A move you seriously consider. Order: checks, captures, threats, then quiet moves. → V.1.

Centipawn (cp). One hundredth of a pawn: the unit of engine evaluation, from the side to move. → V.6.

Checkmate. The side to move is in check and has no legal move. It takes precedence over every draw rule. → RB §8; I.6.

Circuit Grade. A rank of the 16-grade feudal ladder (crown-circuit-grades-1, names proposed), each with sublevels III → II → I: 48 steps from Commoner III to High Sovereign I, two grades per division. Set by your division and by the standing score at two checkpoints a season (after round 8 and at season end), with hysteresis. Your highest rank ever is permanent. Not a rating, not a Federation title. → V.4.

Claim (draw). A request by a player for a draw that is not automatic: threefold repetition or the 100-halfmove rule. → RB §10.

Claim (Exchange). A tradable set of a market's states. A share of the claim pays the sum of the payouts of its states. → VI.2.

Closed (market). No trading is possible; the market awaits settlement or cancellation. Positions in a closed market are valued only at the cancellation vector. → VI.4.

Coach note. An evidence-based explanation attached to an analysed move (coach crown-coach-0), under topics such as Hanging pieces, Knight forks, Mating patterns, Threat awareness, Promotion races and Calculation. → V.5.

Conflict of interest (Exchange). Official markets never list your own games. While you sponsor a competitor, you cannot buy in markets involving them. Entering an event cancels its winner market at 1/n first. → VI (introduction); RB §20.

Critical moment. A position where the best move is at least 0.10 expected score better than the second best, or where a mate is available (crown-critical-1). The summary counts how many you handled (loss ≤ 0.05). → V.5.

Crown scale. The engine-strength rating scale, anchored at L1 = 800 by design. It is not FIDE. → V.3; V.8.

Davidson model. The Federation result model: P(W) ∝ π_w, P(D) ∝ ν√(π_wπ_b), P(B) ∝ π_b, with π = 10^(rating/400) and ν = 0.9 (crown-result-model-1). Used on public ratings for forecasts. → VI.1.

Defensive Survival. Academy mode: find the only move that holds. → V.5.

Division. One of 8 ordered tiers of the Federation: 1 Crown, 2 Grand, 3 Premier, 4 Masters, 5 Senior, 6 District, 7 Club, 8 Open. Each division has 16 regional leagues. → V.4; RB §17.

Endgame Workshop. Academy mode of endgame puzzles, which can then be played out against the engine. → P-Wk 7.

Expected score. The average result (win 1, draw ½, loss 0) a position or pairing is worth. For positions the game uses the map crown-outcome-map-v2 (for example +100 cp ≈ 0.68). For pairings it uses the Davidson model. → V.6; VI.1.

Expected value (EV). The average profit of a trade at your probability: belief × $1 × shares − total paid. → VI.1.

Exposure. The total cost basis at risk in open or closed markets. Correlated positions count together. → VI.4.

Featured game. A Federation engine game chosen for a match market and live spectating. → VI.6.

Fee. 1 % of the executed amount (rounded up) on every buy and every sell. → VI.1.

Federation. The Six-Square Federation: 2,048 AI competitors in 16 regions × 8 divisions × 16-player leagues, with 19 rounds per season. → V.4; RB §§14–17.

Federation title. A permanent honour earned by performance norms: Squire, Knight, Paladin and Sovereign (crown-titles-1). Not a FIDE title, and distinct from rating titles. → V.4; RB §21.

Fivefold repetition. The same position (board and side to move) for the fifth time: an automatic draw. → RB §10.

fullBudget. An engine option (since v0.8) for L8 and L9: keep starting search iterations until 62.5 % of the move's time budget is used. Measured gain: +23 [6, 41] Elo. → V.8.

Glicko-2. The rating system for players and competitors (rating, RD, volatility). New players start at 1500, RD 350. → RB §15.

Grade. The label for a move's expected-score loss (crown-grade-v3-experimental): Best ≤ 0.002, Excellent ≤ 0.02, Good ≤ 0.05, Inaccuracy ≤ 0.12, Mistake ≤ 0.25, Blunder above. The bins are experimental. → V.6.

Hedging. Reducing the spread of possible outcomes, in this game by selling shares you hold (no short selling). It costs fees and slippage. → VI.5.

Highest rank ever achieved. The best Circuit Grade (with sublevel) you have held, with the season it was first reached. Only a genuine step up raises it; demotion, relegation and rating losses never lower it. → V.4.

Implied probability. The probability a price expresses: a $0.40 share implies 40 %. → VI.1.

Kelly criterion. The growth-optimal stake fraction f* = (q − p)/(1 − p) for a $1 claim at price p with belief q. Use fractional Kelly only as a ceiling, never as a target. → VI.4.

Knockout. Crown Championship format: two-game matches, then a rapid pair, then a blitz pair. If still level, the higher seed advances, except in the final, which gives joint champions. → V.4; RB §16.

Lab (Personal Chess Intelligence Lab). Skill dimensions measured as success rates with denominators and 95 % intervals (crown-lab-1). They are performance summaries, not psychometric scores. → V.6.

Latent strength. A competitor's hidden playing strength, which chooses their engine profile. It is never shown, and never used by forecasts or NPC traders. → V.3.

Level (L1–L9). Engine strength profiles (crown-levels-6): L1 Novice … L8 Crown, L9 Sovereign Unbound. → V.3.

Live model. The in-play W/D/B forecast computed from the published engine evaluation and the pre-game draw probability. It is never the price. → VI.6.

LMSR (logarithmic market scoring rule). The automated market maker: C(q) = b·ln Σ e^(qᵢ/b), pᵢ = e^(qᵢ/b)/Σ e^(qⱼ/b), and a trade costs C(q′) − C(q). → VI.2.

Log score. −Σ y·ln max(p, 0.001); lower is better. → VI.3.

Long-only. You can sell only shares you hold. There is no short selling. → VI.5.

Market family. A kind of Exchange market: match, winner, promotion, qualification, season, bracket, sandbox. → VI.5.

Market revision. A counter that advances with every trade and every published live move. A quote from an older revision is rejected. → VI.2; VI.6.

Norm. An event of at least 5 games whose performance rating and average opposition reach a title tier's thresholds. → V.4.

NPC trader. One of eight simulated traders (crown-npc-traders-2) that trade on public information only, with documented noise, bias, margins and budgets. → VI.7.

Opening book (benchmark). The 64 two-ply openings in tools/bench/openings.json, each within ±80 cp at Fairy-Stockfish depth 10. → V.7.

Paper forecast. A free probability vector over a market's states, locked at market close and scored on settlement. → VI.3.

Performance rating. Average opponent rating + dp, with dp = −400·log10(1/p − 1) for score fraction p (±800 cap). → V.4.

Played Like. An estimate of the rating at which a game was played. Shown as "Calibrating": the model failed its release gate (no better than a naive baseline). → V.6.

Playing-length limit. Featured engine games stop at 400 plies. Such a game is censored: its market is cancelled, and the standings record an adjudicated draw, labelled as such. → VI.6.

Promotion (pawn). A pawn reaching the far rank becomes a queen, rook or knight (there are no bishops). It is only four steps from the starting rank. → RB §11; I.9.

Promotion and relegation (league). At season end, the top two of each regional league move up a division and the bottom two move down. → V.4; RB §17.

Provisional rating. A rating with fewer than 20 games or RD > 100. It is excluded from peaks and title collections. → RB §15.

Puzzle Rush. Academy mode: 3 minutes, three strikes. Any solve that is not clean counts as a strike. → P-Wk 2.

Rating pool. A separate rating per timed control (Blitz, Rapid, Classical). → RB §15.

Rating title. A descriptive band of 100 rating points (31 bands, crown-rating-titles-1), from Wandless Wanderer (0–99) to Eternal Sovereign (3000+). It is not a Federation title. → V.4; RB §15.

RD (rating deviation). Glicko-2's uncertainty in a rating. The higher it is, the less the rating means. → V.3.

Regional league. One of the 16 leagues of 16 competitors within each division; a 15-round round robin. → V.4.

Replay Your Mistakes. Academy mode built from your analysed moves that lost ≥ 0.12 expected score. → V.6.

Repertoire (style). The opening preference of a validated style: a choice among book moves within 30 cp of the best at depth 7, for the first six plies only. → V.3.

Retry from This Position (Unrated). Starts an untimed training game from the position before an analysed move, against the same opponent. → V.6.

Sandbox Exchange. Practice markets with separate practice money on your own casual quick matches. You may only back yourself, and trading closes at the first move. → VI (introduction); RB §20.

Settlement. Resolving a market on its result: each winning share pays $1 (joint champions split). → VI.1.

Share. A unit of a claim that pays $1 if the claim's state occurs. → VI.1.

Slippage. The gap between the price shown and the average price paid, caused by your own trade moving the price. → VI.2.

Sonneborn–Berger. A tiebreak: the sum of the scores of the opponents you beat, plus half the scores of those you drew. → V.4.

Sovereign Unbound (L9). The canonical engine with no handicap and a chosen budget of 1/5/10/15/30/60 s per move (rated: 10 s). Rated 3038 ± 171 (derived). → V.8.

Stalemate. The side to move is not in check and has no legal move: a draw. → RB §9; I.7.

Standing score. 0–100 at a Circuit Grade checkpoint: 45 % league position, 25 % score in sanctioned rated games, 30 % rating percentile in your division. → V.4.

Style. A competitor's label (Universal, Tactical, Positional, Defensive, Endgame, Aggressive). Only validated styles change play: Tactical, Positional, Defensive and Endgame, through a whole-game styled evaluation (Tactical and Positional also through an opening repertoire). Aggressive is not validated and plays as Universal. → V.3.

Sublevel. The III / II / I part of a Circuit Grade (III lowest). Shown by one, two or three chevrons under the grade's insignia. → V.4.

Subsidy. The maker's worst-case loss b·ln n, funded before a market opens (match market: $131.83). → VI.2.

Swiss. A pairing system matching players on similar scores who have not met (crown-swiss-1, simplified). → V.4; RB §16.

Threefold repetition. The same position for the third time. The draw is claimable, not automatic. → RB §10.

Timeout rule. If you flag, you lose if your opponent has any non-king piece or pawn; otherwise the game is a draw. → RB §13; V.2.

Training game. An unrated game (for example a retry). It is excluded from the Lab's game evidence. → V.6.

Turning point. A ply where the evaluation crosses between better (> 0.65), balanced and worse (< 0.35). → V.5.

Zugzwang. A position where any move worsens the mover's position. → V.1.
